note.watch: Look for an answer that equals the bottom number of the fraction. Have that child share the pictures into cups first and then lift one cup. Fractions of a group, and fractions written with two numbers, come after second grade: keep saying the words "one third" and treat the page as a first look.

2:2d-attributes.title: Sort shapes by sides
2:2d-attributes.objective: Children count the sides of flat shapes and match each shape to its number of sides.

note.mistake: Children know the regular shapes by sight and are thrown by an irregular one: a five-sided shape that is not a neat pentagon is "not a shape." In a dented shape, a side inside the dent is left out.
note.words: Say: "A shape gets its name from its number of sides, not from how it looks." Name them: "3 sides, triangle. 4 sides, quadrilateral. 5, pentagon. 6, hexagon." Have children mark each side as they count it.
note.watch: Check the shapes with a dent or with one very short side; those are the ones miscounted. Ask for the name of a lopsided four-sided shape and listen for "quadrilateral."

2:flat-or-solid.title: Flat or solid?
2:flat-or-solid.objective: Children sort shapes into flat shapes and solid shapes.

note.mistake: Children call a ball a circle and a box a square: the solid gets the name of its flat face. On paper everything is drawn flat, so the drawing of a cube is sorted as flat.
note.words: Say: "A flat shape lies flat like a piece of paper; it has no thickness. A solid shape can be held; it takes up space." Hold up a real box: "This is a solid. Its FACE is a rectangle." Ask: "Could you pick it up? Could you fill it?"
note.watch: Listen for children who call a ball a circle or a cube a square. Bring real objects; drawings of solids are hard to read for children who have not handled the solids.

2:solids-in-real-life.title: Solid shapes around us
2:solids-in-real-life.objective: Children match a sphere, cube, cylinder, cone, rectangular prism, or pyramid to a real object with the same shape.

note.mistake: Children match by size or color, or by one feature: anything pointed is a cone, so a pyramid and a cone are mixed up. A can lying on its side is not seen as a cylinder. Some still call a ball a circle and a box a square: the solid gets the name of its flat face.
note.words: Name each solid with a thing: "A can is a cylinder. A ball is a sphere. A party hat is a cone." Ask what sets two apart: "A cone's flat bottom is a circle, and its side is curved. A pyramid's flat bottom has straight sides and corners, and its other faces are flat triangles."
note.watch: Go on a solid hunt in the classroom and have children say each name aloud. Check the cone and the pyramid, and the cube and the rectangular prism; those are the pairs children confuse.

2:3d-faces-edges-vertices.title: Faces, edges, and vertices (corners)
2:3d-faces-edges-vertices.objective: Children count the flat faces, the edges, and the corners of solid shapes and write the numbers.

note.mistake: Children count only what they can see in the drawing: three faces of a cube. Going around a solid they lose track and count an edge twice, and they say "side" for a face and for an edge alike.
note.words: Use three words and keep them apart: "A face is a flat surface. An edge is where two faces meet. A corner, or vertex, is where edges meet." On a real box: "Touch a face. Run your finger along an edge. Point to a vertex." For a can or a cone: "Is this part flat or curved? Only the flat parts are faces."
note.watch: Give each pair a real solid and stickers to mark what has been counted. Ask about the hidden parts of a drawing: "What about the back? The bottom?"

2:symmetry-line.title: Is it a line of symmetry?
2:symmetry-line.objective: Children decide whether a dashed line cuts a picture into two matching halves, and pick the picture that is the same on both sides.

note.mistake: Children think any line that cuts a shape into two equal parts is a mirror line. The slanted line across a rectangle makes two equal halves that do not fold onto each other, and children circle the check.
note.words: Say: "A mirror line is a fold line. Fold along it: do the two sides land exactly on top of each other?" Cut out a long paper rectangle (not a square) and fold it corner to corner to show a line that cuts it into two equal parts and is not a mirror line.
note.watch: Use the folding test with paper for the first few. Listen to what children answer for slanted lines; that is where equal halves and mirror halves come apart. Fold a square corner to corner as well, so that "slanted lines are never mirror lines" does not become the rule.

2:symmetry-complete.title: Finish the other half
2:symmetry-complete.objective: Children finish a half-drawn picture so that both sides of the line match like a mirror.

note.mistake: On the grid page children copy the half as it is, sliding it across the line instead of flipping it: a square two boxes from the line is colored two boxes from the far edge. On the tracing page the other half is already there, so children trace without noticing that every part has a partner across the line.
note.words: Say: "Count the boxes AWAY from the line. Two boxes away on this side, two boxes away on the other side." Work row by row. Check with a small mirror on the line: "Does the mirror show what you colored?"
note.watch: Look at the squares farthest from the line; a slid copy puts them next to the line. Give a mirror to any child whose picture looks shifted and let the child find the difference. On the tracing page, have the child point to one part and then to its partner on the other side.

2:tangram-orientation.title: Which one matches the shadow?
2:tangram-orientation.objective: Children compare tangram figures with a shadow and choose the one that stands exactly the same way, not turned and not flipped.

note.mistake: Children pick the first figure made of the same pieces. A figure that is turned or flipped looks "the same" to them, because until now a turned shape always was the same shape.
note.words: Say: "A shape that is turned or flipped is still the same shape. This puzzle asks for more: it must STAND the same way as the shadow." Ask: "Which way does the point face in the shadow? Left or right? Up or down?" Have children trace the outline of the shadow with a finger and then the outline of each choice.
note.watch: Ask a child what is different about a figure they did not choose: "It is flipped" or "It is turned." Naming the difference is the skill; the match alone can be a lucky guess.

3:compare-4-digit.title: Compare four-digit numbers
3:compare-4-digit.objective: Children compare two four-digit numbers place by place from the left and circle the sign for greater than, less than, or equal.

note.mistake: Children compare the first digits and guess when those match, or they are drawn to big digits at the end: 3,099 looks greater than 3,100. A number with zeros inside is misread, 4,007 as "four hundred seven."
note.words: Say: "Read both numbers aloud first. Then start on the left: thousands, hundreds, tens, ones. Stop at the first place where they differ." Ask: "Which place decided it?"
note.watch: Have the child name the place that decided each comparison. Check pairs that differ only in the tens or the ones, and numbers with zeros; reading a number aloud shows whether its places are understood.

3:rounding.title: Round to the nearest hundred
3:rounding.objective: Children find which hundred a number is closer to on a number line and round three-digit numbers to the nearest hundred.

note.mistake: Children look at the ones digit, as they did when rounding to ten, so 349 is rounded up to 400 because of the 9. Or they change only the tens and write 350.
note.words: Ask: "Which two hundreds is 349 between? What number is halfway?" (350.) "Is 349 before or after halfway?" Say: "For hundreds, the TENS digit decides. The ones do not matter."
note.watch: Use 349 and 351 as test numbers. A child who rounds both the same way is not thinking of the halfway point; put both numbers on a line from 300 to 400.

3:column-regrouping.title: Add and subtract with regrouping
3:column-regrouping.objective: Children add and subtract in columns within 1,000, regrouping when a place has more than nine or not enough to take away.

note.mistake: Children forget to add the new ten or hundred, or they write it and add it twice. In subtraction they trade a ten for ten ones and forget to make the tens one smaller; with a zero in the tens place (402 − 178) they do not know where the ten ones can come from.
note.words: Say each step: "8 and 7 is 15 ones. That is 1 ten and 5 ones. Write the 5, and write the new ten above the tens." For a zero: "No tens to trade. Go to the hundreds: trade one hundred for ten tens. Now trade one of those tens for ten ones."
note.watch: Check subtraction across a zero first. Have children add the answer back to check a subtraction, and ask "About how much should it be?" before they compute.

3:estimate-by-rounding.title: Round, then estimate the sum
3:estimate-by-rounding.objective: Children round two numbers to the nearest ten and add the rounded numbers to estimate the sum; with the teacher, they use an estimate to judge whether an exact answer is reasonable.

note.mistake: Children work out the exact sum first and then round the answer, which defeats the purpose. Or they round only one of the two numbers.
note.words: Say: "Round first, then add. An estimate is fast and close, not exact." Show it: "48 + 31 is about 50 + 30. About 80." Then: "Someone got 109 for 48 + 31. Can that be right? How do you know without adding?"
note.watch: See who writes the exact sum in the margin before rounding. Give a wrong exact answer and ask the class to catch it with an estimate; that is what estimating is for.

3:parity-of-sums.title: Is the sum odd or even?
3:parity-of-sums.objective: Children decide whether a sum will be odd or even by looking at the ones digits of the two numbers, without adding.

note.mistake: Children add anyway and then look at the answer. Or they guess a rule that feels right: "odd plus odd must be odd."
note.words: Try small numbers first and collect the results: "3 + 5 = 8. Odd plus odd… even!" Ask why: "Each odd number has one left over. The two leftovers make a pair." Build the three rules together: even + even, odd + odd, even + odd.
note.watch: Ask a child to explain odd plus odd with counters laid out in pairs. A child who can only recite the table will forget it; one who sees the two leftovers pair up will not.

3:arithmetic-patterns.title: Find the rule of a number pattern
3:arithmetic-patterns.objective: Children find how much a number pattern grows or shrinks at each step and write the missing numbers.

note.mistake: Children look at one pair of numbers, decide on a rule, and do not test it on the rest of the row. In shrinking patterns they keep adding. Two missing numbers in a row stop them.
note.words: Ask: "How do you get from this number to the next? Is it the same jump every time? Check it on three pairs." Have children write the rule above the row: "+ 25" or "− 4." For a double gap: "Two jumps take you from 40 to 60. How big is one jump?"
note.watch: See who writes the rule down and tests it. Mix growing and shrinking rows; a child who adds in a shrinking row has stopped looking at the numbers.

3:mult-equal-groups.title: Multiplication as equal groups
3:mult-equal-groups.objective: Children read a picture of equal groups or an array, finish the multiplication, and find the total.

note.mistake: Children count every picture by ones and never use the groups. In the equation they write the total where a factor belongs.
note.words: Say: "6 groups of 4 is 6 times 4." Find the total from a fact you know: "5 groups of 4 is 20, one more group is 24." Use the words "factor" for the numbers you multiply and "product" for the total.
note.watch: Ask how the child found the total. Counting by ones gives a right answer and no progress; a child who says "five of them and one more" is building the tables.

3:mult-number-line.title: Multiplication hops
3:mult-number-line.objective: Children show a multiplication as equal hops from zero on a number line and write the number where each hop lands.

note.mistake: Children write the number of the hop (1, 2, 3) under each landing and not the place where it lands. Or they start the first hop at 1, so that every landing is one too big.
note.words: Say: "Every hop is the same size. Start at zero. Hops of 4 land on 4, 8, 12." Ask: "How many hops? How big is each one? Where are you after 5 hops of 4?" Call the landing numbers "multiples of 4."
note.watch: Check that the first landing equals the size of the hop. Ask for "3 hops of 5" and "5 hops of 3" and let children see that both end in the same place.

3:commutative.title: Turn the array around
3:commutative.objective: Children see that an array turned on its side shows the same total, and write both multiplication equations.

note.mistake: Children count both arrays from scratch as two separate problems and do not notice that the totals match. Some believe 3 × 7 and 7 × 3 are two different facts that both have to be learned.
note.words: Turn a paper array a quarter turn and ask: "Did I add any? Did I take any away? So what is the total now?" Say: "3 rows of 7 and 7 rows of 3 are the same amount. If you know one, you know the other."
note.watch: Ask "What is 7 × 3?" right after a child has worked out 3 × 7. A child who starts counting again has not taken in the turn; turn the array once more.

3:times-tables.title: Multiplication facts for 2 and 5
3:times-tables.objective: Children write the products for the 2 and 5 times tables and practice a mix of multiplication facts.

note.mistake: Children skip count from the start for every fact and lose track around the sixth or seventh number. They mix up neighbors: 6 × 5 is answered with 35.
note.words: Start from a fact the child knows: "You know 5 × 5 is 25. So 6 × 5 is one more five: 30." Use doubles for the 2s, and half of the tens fact for the 5s: "8 × 10 is 80, so 8 × 5 is half of that, 40."
note.watch: Listen for how a child gets a fact: from memory, from a neighbor fact, or by counting from the start. Practice a few facts each day; a page finished by skip counting has not built memory.

3:division-sharing.title: Divide by sharing
3:division-sharing.objective: Children share a pile equally into a given number of bins and write how many each bin gets.

note.mistake: Children write the number of bins or the size of the pile as the answer. Without counters they guess how many go in each bin and do not check that the bins use up the pile.
note.words: Say: "12 shared among 3 is a division: 12 ÷ 3." Then deal: "One for each, again, again, until none are left. Each gets 4." Check with multiplication: "3 bins of 4 make 12." Read the sign as "divided by."
note.watch: Ask every child to check one answer by multiplying. A child who sees that 3 × 4 = 12 answers 12 ÷ 3 has found the shortcut that makes division easy.

3:division-repeated-subtraction.title: Divide by hopping back
3:division-repeated-subtraction.objective: Children find how many equal hops it takes to get from a number back to zero on a number line.

note.mistake: Children write the size of the hop as the answer, or they count every mark they touch, the starting number included, which gives one too many. They do not see that this is division too.
note.words: Say: "Start at 15. Hop back 3 each time: 12, 9, 6, 3, 0. How many hops? Five." Write it: "15 ÷ 3 = 5. There are five 3s in 15." Ask: "How many 3s fit into 15?"
note.watch: Have children count hops with a finger on each arc, not on the marks. Put the two meanings side by side once: 15 shared among 3, and how many 3s are in 15.

3:mult-div-relationship.title: The missing factor and fact families
3:mult-div-relationship.objective: Children find the missing factor of an array and write the two multiplications and the two divisions that belong to it.

note.mistake: Children treat a division as a new problem and do not use the multiplication they just wrote. In a fact family they write a division that starts with a small number, such as 4 ÷ 24 = 6.
note.words: Say: "Division asks for the missing factor. 24 ÷ 4 asks: 4 times what is 24?" Point to the array: "In a fact family the total is the number we divide: 24 ÷ 4, not 4 ÷ 24." Have children read all four facts of one array aloud.
note.watch: Ask a division and see whether the child thinks of the multiplication. Check the order of the numbers in each division: the total, the whole array, comes first. Say "the total," never "the biggest number"; later on children will divide a smaller number by a bigger one.

3:muldiv-word-problems.title: Multiplication and division word problems
3:muldiv-word-problems.objective: Children solve word problems with equal groups, deciding whether the story asks for the total, for the size of each group, or for the number of groups.

note.mistake: Children pick out the two numbers and multiply every time, or choose the operation from one word such as "each." They do not ask what the answer will be: a total, a share, or a number of groups.
note.words: Ask three questions about every story: "Do we know how many groups? Do we know how many in each group? Do we know the total?" Then: "Which of the three is missing?" Have children finish with a sentence: "Each child gets 4 stickers."
note.watch: Read a child's answer sentence, not only the number. A bare "4" does not show whether the child knows it is 4 stickers each or 4 bags. Each page holds one kind of story, so the page decides for the child: read one story from each page aloud, in mixed order and without the picture, and ask which of the three is missing.

3:balance-equations.title: Make it balance
3:balance-equations.objective: Children use the equal sign as a balance and write the number that makes both sides the same amount.

note.mistake: Children read the equal sign as "the answer comes next." In 8 + 4 = __ + 5 they write 12 in the blank, or 17 by adding everything.
note.words: Say: "The equal sign means the SAME on both sides, like a balance." Work out one side first: "8 + 4 is 12. So the other side must be 12 too. What plus 5 makes 12?" Read the sign as "is the same as."
note.watch: Give three quick true-or-false cards: 7 = 7, 5 + 3 = 3 + 5, 12 = 8 + 4. A child who calls them wrong "because the answer is on the wrong side" still reads the sign as "the answer comes next"; that child should work with a real or a drawn balance and smaller numbers.

3:division-remainder.title: Division with a remainder
3:division-remainder.objective: Children make equal groups from a pile or deal it into boxes, write how many groups there are or how many each box gets, and write how many are left over.

note.mistake: Children leave too many over: as many as a group or more on the grouping page, as many as the number of boxes or more on the sharing page, when one more group or one more round could be made. Or they drop the leftovers and write only the number of groups.
note.words: Say: "14 in groups of 4: three groups, and 2 left over." Ask: "Can you make another group from what is left? No? Then that is the remainder." On the sharing page: "14 into 4 boxes. Is there enough left to give every box one more?" State the rule together: "The remainder is always smaller than the number you divide by."
note.watch: Check each remainder against the number the pile was divided by: the size of a group on the grouping page, the number of boxes on the sharing page. A remainder of 5 with groups of 4 means one group is still hiding in the leftovers. Remainders are a fourth-grade standard: keep the words "left over" and treat this lesson as a first look.

3:time-to-minute.title: Tell time to the minute
3:time-to-minute.objective: Children read an analog clock to the exact minute and choose the matching time.

note.mistake: Children read to the nearest five and stop, so 4:23 is called 4:20 or 4:25. Others count every small mark from the 12 and lose count on the way around.
note.words: Say: "Go to the number just before the minute hand and count by fives to it: 5, 10, 15, 20. Then count the small marks one by one: 21, 22, 23." Ask: "Is the hour hand past the 4? A little or a lot?"
note.watch: Listen to a child count: fives first, then ones. Check times in the last quarter of the hour, where the hour hand is close to the next number.

3:add-subtract-time.title: Add and subtract time
3:add-subtract-time.objective: Children start at a clock time, add or subtract minutes or hours, and write the new time.

note.mistake: Children add the minutes as plain numbers and write a time that does not exist, such as 3:75. Going back across the hour, they change the minutes and forget to change the hour.
note.words: Say: "An hour has 60 minutes, not 100." Jump to the full hour first: "3:45 plus 30 minutes. 15 minutes takes us to 4:00. 15 more: 4:15." Draw the jumps on an open number line with the times written on it.
note.watch: Look for minutes of 60 or more in an answer. Have children show the jump to the next full hour on a clock or on a line before they write.

3:elapsed-duration.title: How much time passed?
3:elapsed-duration.objective: Children compare two clock times and find how much time passed between them.

note.mistake: Children subtract the two clock numbers without thinking about the clock: from 11:00 to 2:00 becomes 9 hours. Or they count the starting hour as the first hour.
note.words: Say: "Count the jumps from the start time to the end time: 11 to 12 is one hour, 12 to 1 is two, 1 to 2 is three." Ask: "Does three hours make sense? What could you do in that time?"
note.watch: Check the items that pass 12 o'clock. A child who writes 9 hours for 11:00 to 2:00 subtracted; go around a real clock together and count each hour as it passes.

3:time-12-24.title: 12-hour and 24-hour time
3:time-12-24.objective: Children match a time on the 12-hour clock to the same time on the 24-hour clock.

note.mistake: Children add 12 to morning times as well, or they drop the first digit, so that 15:00 becomes 5:00. Noon and midnight are confused.
note.words: Say: "After 12 noon the 24-hour clock keeps counting: 13, 14, 15." Give the rule both ways: "From 1:00 p.m. to 11:59 p.m., add 12 to the hour. From 24-hour time: if the hour is more than 12, subtract 12 and say p.m." Ask: "Is 08:00 morning or evening? How do you know?"
note.watch: Check noon and the hour after it, such as 12:30 p.m., which stays 12:30, and midnight, which is 00:00. Most clocks around the children show a.m. and p.m.; point out a bus schedule or a plane ticket that uses 24-hour time. This lesson goes beyond the Common Core; many Americans know 24-hour time as "military time."

3:thermometer.title: Read a thermometer
3:thermometer.objective: Children read the temperature on a thermometer whose scale counts by 2, by 5, or by 10.

note.mistake: Children count every mark as one degree, whatever the scale. They read the nearest printed number and ignore the marks between, or look at the top of the tube and not at the top of the colored line.
note.words: Ask first: "This scale does not count by ones. What do the printed numbers count by? So what is each small mark worth?" Then: "Find the top of the line. Which printed number is just below it? Count up from there." Say the temperature with its unit, as the page prints it: "70 degrees."
note.watch: Compare two thermometers with different scales that show the same temperature, and ask which one was harder to read and why.

3:area-model.title: Area: count the squares
3:area-model.objective: Children find the area of a rectangle by counting its squares in rows and finish the multiplication for it.

note.mistake: Children count the squares one by one and miscount in a big rectangle. Others count the squares along two sides and add them, which gives a number that has nothing to do with the area.
note.words: Say: "Area is how many squares cover the shape with no gaps and no overlaps." Ask: "How many squares in one row? How many rows? 4 rows of 6 is 24 squares." Say the unit: "24 square units."
note.watch: Ask how the child counted. Rows times columns is the goal; counting one by one is the starting point. Listen for the word "square" in the unit.

3:same-area.title: Same area, different shape
3:same-area.objective: Children compare rectangles and circle the one that covers the same number of squares as another.

note.mistake: Children choose the rectangle that looks most like the first one, or think a long thin rectangle must be bigger than a compact one. They judge by eye and do not count.
note.words: Say: "Different shape, same space. Count the squares of each one." Ask: "A 2 by 6 and a 3 by 4. How many squares in each?" Cut a 3 by 4 paper rectangle into pieces and rearrange it: "Did the area change?"
note.watch: See who counts and who goes by looks. Ask a child to draw two different rectangles with 12 squares on grid paper.

3:perimeter.title: Perimeter: walk the edge
3:perimeter.objective: Children find the perimeter of a rectangle by counting the unit edges all the way around.

note.mistake: Children count the squares along the border and not the edges, so a corner square is counted once where it has two outside edges. Or they count the squares inside and give the area.
note.words: Say: "Perimeter is the distance around, like a fence." Walk a finger along the outside: "Count the edges, not the squares. Mark where you start." For a rectangle: "Two long sides and two short sides: 5 + 3 + 5 + 3."
note.watch: Check the corners: a child who counts squares gets a number that is 4 too small. Ask "Is that the fence or the grass?" to keep perimeter and area apart.

3:same-perimeter.title: Same perimeter, different area
3:same-perimeter.objective: Children compare rectangles and circle the one with the same distance around as another.

note.mistake: Children believe that rectangles with the same perimeter must have the same area, or they compare areas because counting squares is what they did last. A long thin rectangle is judged to have the longer fence.
note.words: Say: "Same fence, new yard." Make a loop of string and pull it into different rectangles: "The string did not get longer. Did the space inside stay the same?" Have children count the edges of each rectangle and write the numbers.
note.watch: Ask for both numbers of two rectangles, the perimeter and the area, and have the child say which is which. This lesson exists to pull the two ideas apart.

3:partition-equal-areas.title: Equal pieces
3:partition-equal-areas.objective: Children decide whether a shape is cut into equal parts; with the teacher, they name one of the equal parts as a unit fraction.

note.mistake: This page reviews second grade. Children count the parts and do not compare them: four parts are "fourths" even when the parts differ in size. Parts that are equal in size and different in shape are turned down.
note.words: Ask: "Does every part cover the same amount?" Say: "Only equal parts get a fraction name. Four EQUAL parts: each one is one fourth." Show a square cut into four triangles and one cut into four small squares: "Different shapes, same amount."
note.watch: Look at the circles with one thin slice and the rectangles with unequal strips. A child who circles them is counting parts. Cut paper and lay the parts on top of each other; when two parts have different shapes, cut one of them and rearrange its pieces to cover the other.

3:fraction-unit-build.title: Name and shade a fraction
3:fraction-unit-build.objective: Children write the fraction that the shaded parts of a shape show, and shade a shape to show a given fraction.

note.mistake: Children write the shaded parts over the unshaded parts: 3 shaded and 1 not becomes 3/1. Or they turn the fraction upside down, with the number of all the parts on top.
note.words: Say: "The bottom number tells how many equal parts the whole has. The top number tells how many of them we mean." Count unit pieces: "One fourth, two fourths, three fourths." Use "numerator" and "denominator" once children have the idea.
note.watch: Check a shape with 3 of 4 parts shaded. The answer 3/1 means the child compared shaded with unshaded; count all the parts together first, then the shaded ones.

3:whole-from-unit.title: Find the whole
3:whole-from-unit.objective: Children look at one equal part and choose the bar that shows the whole it came from.

note.mistake: Children choose the longest bar, or a bar as long as the part itself. They do not use the fraction to tell how many parts make the whole.
note.words: Say: "This piece is one third. How many thirds make a whole? Three. So the whole is three of these pieces long." Have children lay the piece down again and again, or mark its length along the bar.
note.watch: Ask "How many of these pieces fit in the whole?" before the child circles. The answer should match the bottom number of the fraction.

3:compare-fractions.title: Which fraction is greater?
3:compare-fractions.objective: Children compare two fractions of the same whole with fraction bars and circle the greater one.

note.mistake: Children think a bigger bottom number means a bigger fraction: one eighth is taken to be more than one fourth, because 8 is more than 4.
note.words: Ask: "Would you get more pizza if it is shared among 4 people or among 8?" Say: "More parts means smaller parts." With the same bottom number: "Three fifths and two fifths: the pieces are the same size, so more pieces is more." Always add: "We can only compare fractions of wholes that are the same size."
note.watch: Use 1/4 and 1/8 as the test. A child who picks 1/8 is comparing whole numbers; go back to two equal bars, one cut into fourths and one into eighths.

3:equivalent-fractions.title: Equivalent fractions: different names, same amount
3:equivalent-fractions.objective: Children match a picture to a fraction that shows the same amount, such as one half and two fourths.

note.mistake: Children look for a fraction with the same numbers as the picture and find none. Two fractions with different numbers cannot be equal, they think, so 1/2 and 2/4 are different amounts.
note.words: Fold a paper strip in half, then in half again: "One half is the same amount as two fourths. Nothing was added." Say: "Different name, same amount. We call them equivalent fractions." Ask: "How many sixths cover the same space as one half?"
note.watch: Have children lay two fraction strips one above the other and compare where the shading ends. A child who needs the numbers to match should fold paper before working on the page.

3:right-angles.title: Right angles
3:right-angles.objective: Children find the right angles, the square corners, of shapes and circle them.

note.mistake: Children see a right angle only when one arm lies flat and the other stands up. A square corner on a tilted shape is missed, and an angle that is nearly square is accepted.
note.words: Give each child a "corner checker," the corner of an index card: "Fit the card into the angle. Does it fit exactly? Then it is a right angle." Use "smaller than a right angle" and "bigger than a right angle."
note.watch: See who turns the card or the page to test a tilted corner. Check the angles that are almost right angles; only the card can settle those.

3:classify-quadrilaterals.title: Is it a rectangle?
3:classify-quadrilaterals.objective: Children decide whether a four-sided shape is a rectangle by checking its sides and its angles, knowing that a square is also a rectangle.

note.mistake: Children say a square is not a rectangle because "a rectangle has two long sides and two short sides." A tilted rectangle is not accepted, and a leaning parallelogram is taken for one.
note.words: Ask: "What makes a rectangle? Four sides and four right angles." Then: "Does a square have four sides and four right angles? Then it is a rectangle, a special one." Test corners with the corner of a card.
note.watch: Ask "Is a square a rectangle?" and listen for the reason. A child who says "yes, because it has four right angles" is sorting by properties, which is the point of the lesson.

3:symmetry.title: How many lines of symmetry?
3:symmetry.objective: Children find all the lines of symmetry of a shape and write how many there are.

note.mistake: Children find the up-and-down line and stop. They miss the line across and the slanted ones, or they count the diagonals of a long rectangle, which are not mirror lines.
note.words: Say: "Try every fold: up and down, across, corner to corner." Use cut-out shapes: "Fold it. Do the halves match exactly?" Ask: "A square has 4 mirror lines. Why does a rectangle that is not a square have only 2?"
note.watch: Hand out paper shapes to fold. Check the long rectangle: a child who writes 4 for it has not folded it along a diagonal.

3:scaled-graphs.title: Graphs with a scale
3:scaled-graphs.objective: Children read bar graphs whose scale counts by 5 and pictographs in which each picture stands for 5.

note.mistake: Children count the grid lines or the pictures as ones and ignore the scale. A bar that ends at a line with no number is read as the printed number below it.
note.words: Ask first: "What does the scale count by? What does one picture stand for?" Count along: "5, 10, 15, 20." For a bar that stops at a line with no number: "The printed numbers on each side are 10 and 20. What is this line worth?"
note.watch: Have the child read the key or the scale aloud before the first answer. Ask one compare question ("how many more") to see whether the child uses the scaled numbers or counts pictures.

3:line-plot-halves.title: A line plot with halves
3:line-plot-halves.objective: Children read a line plot whose number line is marked in halves and write how many X marks stand above each number.

note.mistake: Children skip the half marks and read only the whole numbers, moving an X at 2½ to 2 or to 3. They also mix up the measurement under a stack with the number of Xs in it.
note.words: Read the line aloud together: "1, one and a half, 2, two and a half." Ask: "How many things were two and a half units long? Count the Xs above that mark." Then: "How many were longer than 2?"
note.watch: Ask a question whose answer sits on a half mark. A child who answers for the nearest whole number is not yet reading the halves on the line.

K:pre-writing-strokes.title: Lines, zigzags, and curves
K:pre-writing-strokes.objective: Children trace straight lines, zigzags, waves, and curves from the starting dot in the direction of the arrow.

note.mistake: Children start wherever the pencil lands and trace against the arrow, or they lift the pencil at every bend. Many hold the pencil in a fist and press so hard that the hand is tired after two lines.
note.words: Say: "Find the orange dot. That is where the pencil starts. Follow the arrow and do not lift until the line ends." For the grip: "Pinch the pencil with your thumb and pointer finger; let it rest on your middle finger." Name each stroke as the child traces it: "straight across, zigzag, wave, curve around."
note.watch: Watch the starting point and the direction, not how neat the line is. A child who starts at the wrong end or traces against the arrow here will form letters the same way; correct it now, one line at a time, by putting the child's finger on the orange dot before the pencil goes down.

K:letter-identification.title: Find the letter
K:letter-identification.objective: Children find every copy of a letter among letters that look like it, such as b, d, p, and q.

note.mistake: Children circle b, d, p, and q as the same letter: a stick and a ball. Turning a toy does not change what it is, so they do not expect turning a letter to change it.
note.words: Say: "Letters are special. Turn a b around and it is a different letter." Give each one a short cue and keep it all year: "b: stick first, then the ball. d: ball first, then the stick. p: the stick hangs down below the line, then the ball. q: ball first, then the stick hangs down." Ask: "What comes first, the stick or the ball? Does the stick go up or hang down?"
note.watch: Have the child name each letter they circle. A child who circles correctly and cannot name the letters is matching shapes; one who names d as b needs the cue, not more circling.

K:letter-case.title: Uppercase and lowercase letters
K:letter-case.objective: Children match each capital letter to its small letter.

note.mistake: Children match the pairs that look alike (C c, S s, O o) and guess at the ones that do not: A a, G g, R r, Q q. The small letters b, d, p, and q get the wrong partners.
note.words: Say: "Every letter has two shapes, a capital and a small one. We also call them uppercase and lowercase. They have the same name and stand for the same sound." Point to both: "Capital G, small g." Ask: "Which pairs look alike? Which look different?"
note.watch: Note which pairs each child misses and practice only those. The pairs that look different have to be learned one at a time; there is no trick for them.

K:letter-formation.title: Write the letters
K:letter-formation.objective: Children trace each letter from its starting dot in the direction of the arrows and write one on their own.

note.mistake: Children draw letters from the bottom up or in pieces, so that an M is four lines drawn in any order and an O goes around the wrong way. The letter looks right on the page, and the habit slows writing later.
note.words: Say the path aloud for each letter and use the same words every time: "Capital B: down, back to the top, around, around." Ask: "Where does it start? Which way does the arrow go first?" Write the letter big in the air together before the pencil touches the page.
note.watch: Stand where you can see the hand moving. Check the letter the child writes alone on the empty line; that one shows whether the path was learned or only followed.

K:alphabet-order.title: The alphabet in order
K:alphabet-order.objective: Children say the alphabet in order, write the letters that are missing, and connect dots in alphabet order.

note.mistake: Children can sing the alphabet and cannot say what comes after a letter in the middle without starting from A. "L, M, N, O, P" is sung as one word, so those letters get lost.
note.words: Say the alphabet slowly while pointing to each letter, and stop: "…F, G. What comes next?" Ask: "What comes after K? What comes before K?" Slow down at "L, M, N, O, P" and tap each letter.
note.watch: Notice who sings from A for every gap. Keep an alphabet strip on the desk for those children and have them find a letter and its neighbors by looking, then from memory.

K:word-sentence-tracing.title: Trace and write words
K:word-sentence-tracing.objective: Children trace a short word, read it, and write it on their own from left to right.

note.mistake: Children trace the letters in any order and never read the word, so the page becomes drawing practice. When they write the word alone, they leave out a letter, change the order of the letters, or spread the letters so far apart that the word looks like two.
note.words: Say: "Read it first. Now trace it, and say each sound as you trace its letter. Now write it and read it again." For a sight word that does not sound out: "Spell it as you trace: t-h-e, the." For spacing: "Letters in one word sit close together, like friends. If you write the word twice, leave a finger space between."
note.watch: Ask the child to read back what was written. Look at the word written alone: are the letters in order, close together, and sitting on the line?

K:all-about-me-personal.title: All about me
K:all-about-me-personal.objective: Children write their name and age, draw themselves and their favorite things, and copy the words for things they like.

note.mistake: Children write their name in all capitals or with letters out of order, and some cannot yet write the numeral for their age. Copying a word, they skip a letter or lose their place and start it over.
note.words: Say: "Your name starts with a capital letter. The other letters are small." For copying: "Look at the first letter. Write it. Look at the next one." Ask each child about the drawing: "Tell me about your picture."
note.watch: This page has no wrong answers about the child's life; correct only the name and the copied words. Listen to what children say about their drawings, and write their words under the picture if they ask.

K:word-picture-match.title: Match words to pictures
K:word-picture-match.objective: Children read a short word and match it to the picture it names.

note.mistake: Children look at the first letter only and take the first picture that starts with it: "cat" is matched to the cup. Or they name the pictures and guess at the words by their length.
note.words: Say: "Touch each letter and say its sound. Now say the sounds fast. What word is it?" Then: "Does the word end the way the picture's name ends? Check the last sound."
note.watch: Listen to a child sound out one word. A child who says the first sound and then names a picture is guessing; cover the pictures and have the word read first.

K:sight-words-reading.title: Sight words
K:sight-words-reading.objective: Children read a common word at a glance, find it among words that look like it, and write it in a sentence.

note.mistake: Children mix up words that look alike (was and saw, on and no, the and they). With a word that has one irregular part, they sound out that part as it is spelled, say "sayd" for said or "wass" for was, and do not notice that it is not a word they know.
note.words: Say: "Sound out the parts that play by the rules. One part you have to know by heart." Point to that part: "In 'said,' s and d say their sounds; the a-i says /e/, and that is the heart part." For a word with no tricky part: "This one plays by the rules all the way: /o/ /n/, on." Have children read the word, spell it aloud, and read it again: "said, s-a-i-d, said."
note.watch: Check the look-alike boxes on the coloring page: they show which words a child confuses. Have the child read the finished sentences aloud; writing the word in is not the same as reading it.

K:digraphs-k.title: sh and ch
K:digraphs-k.objective: Children say a picture's name and decide whether it begins with the sound of sh or the sound of ch.

note.mistake: Children hear /sh/ and /ch/ as the same sound, or say one for the other: "shair" for chair, "chip" for ship. This is most common in children whose home language has only one of the two sounds, such as Spanish. Others name the picture with a different word (boat for ship) and then cannot find its sound.
note.words: Say: "Two letters, one sound. sh says /sh/, the quiet sound. ch says /ch/, like a sneeze." Stretch the first sound: "shhhh-ip." You can hold /sh/; you cannot hold /ch/. Ask: "Can you hold the sound?"
note.watch: Name every picture together before anyone draws a line, so that all children sort the same words. Have each child say the word before drawing the line. A child who sorts by looking and not by saying will not hear the difference; say the pairs together and feel the mouth: ship, chip; shoe, chew.

K:singular-plural.title: One and many
K:singular-plural.objective: Children tell the word for one from the word for more than one and write the plural with s.

note.mistake: Children say the plural when they talk and leave the s off when they write. They have not noticed that the s at the end is what tells "more than one."
note.words: Say: "One cat. Two cats. What did I add? Listen to the end." Have children say both and hold the last sound: "cats-s-s." Tell them once: "In 'dogs' the end sounds like /z/, but we still write s." Ask: "Is it one or more than one? Does your word have its s?"
note.watch: Read the child's written plural and check the last letter. Irregular plurals (feet, mice) come later; if a child says "foots," accept it for now and say the right word back.

K:articles.title: A or an?
K:articles.objective: Children say a picture word aloud and choose a or an to go in front of it.

note.mistake: Children always circle "a," or they guess. They have not noticed that "a apple" is hard to say, because nobody has asked them to listen for it.
note.words: Say both and let children hear it: "a apple… an apple. Which one is easier to say?" Give the rule in child words: "If the word starts with a vowel sound, like the first sound in apple, egg, igloo, octopus, or umbrella, use an." Have them say the whole pair: "an egg, a dog."
note.watch: Make sure children say the words aloud; this page cannot be done silently at this age. For children who speak another language at home, a and an may be new and need more spoken practice.

K:category-sort.title: Sort into groups
K:category-sort.objective: Children decide which group each picture belongs to, such as animals or food, and sort the pictures.

note.mistake: Children put things together because they go together in life (the dog with the bone) and not because they are the same kind of thing. Asked why, they tell a story about the two pictures.
note.words: Name the group before sorting: "This bin is for animals. Is a dog an animal? Is a bone an animal?" Ask for the group word: "A dog, a cat, and a cow are all…?" Use "belongs" and "kind of": "A carrot is a kind of food."
note.watch: Ask "Why does it go there?" for one picture per child. "Because it is an animal" names a category; "because the dog eats it" tells a story. Both are thinking; only the first is sorting.

K:category-odd-one-out.title: Which one does not belong?
K:category-odd-one-out.objective: Children look at a row of pictures, find the one that is not the same kind of thing, and say why.

note.mistake: Children circle the picture that looks different (the biggest one, the only red one) when the row is about kinds of things. Or they circle one and cannot say what the other three have in common.
note.words: Ask: "What are these three? They are all fruit. Is the shoe a fruit?" Have the child finish the sentence: "The shoe does not belong because…" Accept another answer if the reason is good, and say so.
note.watch: The reason matters more than the circle. A child who gives a different answer with a sound reason has done the thinking; ask the class whether they can see it that way too.

K:opposites.title: Opposites
K:opposites.objective: Children match a picture to the picture that shows its opposite, such as big and small or hot and cold.

note.mistake: Children match two pictures that go together (hot and the sun, night and a bed) and not two that are opposite. Or they join a picture to the nearest picture without looking at the word printed with it.
note.words: Act them out: "Stand up… sit down. Open… shut." Say: "Opposites are as different as they can be." Ask with a sentence to finish: "The soup is hot. The ice is…?"
note.watch: Have children say both words of each pair they join. A child who can act out the opposite and cannot name it needs the words; that is a vocabulary matter, not a thinking one.

K:story-sequencing.title: First, next, last
K:story-sequencing.objective: Children look at the pictures of a short story and put them in the order in which things happen.

note.mistake: Children number the pictures from left to right as they are printed, without looking at what happens in them. Or they find the first picture and guess the other two.
note.words: Ask: "What is different in this picture? What happened before that?" Tell the story with the three words: "FIRST the seed is in the ground. NEXT a leaf comes up. LAST there is a flower." Have the child tell it back the same way.
note.watch: Have each child tell the story aloud from the finished page. If the telling makes sense, the order is right; a child who cannot tell it has numbered boxes, not ordered a story.

1:rhyming.title: Rhyming words
1:rhyming.objective: Children say picture words aloud, find the ones that rhyme, and write the rhyming words.

note.mistake: Children match words that start with the same sound (cat and cup) and call it a rhyme. Others go by spelling and miss rhymes that are spelled differently, such as bear and chair.
note.words: Say: "Rhyming words sound the same from the middle to the end. Only the beginning changes. Cat, hat. Listen: -at, -at." Have children say both words and then only the part after the first sound. Ask: "Cat and cup: say the parts after /k/. -at, -up. Are they the same?"
note.watch: Have each child say the pair aloud before circling; rhyming is done with the ears, not the eyes. A child who keeps picking the same first sound should hear and say endings before writing anything.

1:phoneme-boxes.title: Sound boxes
1:phoneme-boxes.objective: Children say a word slowly, write one sound in each box, and blend the sounds in the boxes back into a word.

note.mistake: Children write one letter in each box and not one sound, so "ship" takes four boxes. Or they leave out a sound in the middle, most often the vowel, and write "shp."
note.words: Say: "Stretch the word like a rubber band: sh-i-p. How many sounds? Three. sh is two letters and ONE sound; it shares a box." For blending: "Say each sound, then say them faster, then say the word."
note.watch: Count the boxes a child fills for a word with a letter team. Listen to the blending: a child who says the sounds correctly and then names a different word is guessing from the first sound.

1:digraphs.title: sh, ch, and th
1:digraphs.objective: Children hear which letter team a picture word has, sh, ch, or th, and write the missing team in the word.

note.mistake: Children mix up th with f or d ("fumb," "dis") because that is how they say the words. They write a single letter for the team: "s" for sh, "c" for ch.
note.words: Say: "A letter team is two letters that make one new sound." Show the mouth for th: "Put your tongue between your teeth and blow: th, as in thumb. Now turn your voice on: th, as in this. Same letters, same tongue." Compare: "Thumb. Not fumb. Feel your tongue."
note.watch: Listen to how each child says the th words; a child who says /f/ or /d/ will write f or d. Use a small mirror for th. If that is how the child's family says the word, do not call the speech wrong; teach that the word is spelled with th. On the writing page, check that both letters of the team are there.

1:spell-picture-words.title: Spell the picture word
1:spell-picture-words.objective: Children say a picture word, listen for its sounds, and write the word, first with the first letter given and then on their own.

note.mistake: Children write the first and the last sound and skip the middle: "ct" for cat, "fg" for frog. Short vowels are mixed up, e and i most of all ("pin" for pen). Where pin and pen are said alike, as in much of the South, a child cannot hear the difference and has to learn which words take e.
note.words: Say: "Say the word slowly. Tap each sound on your fingers. Write the letter or the letter team for every tap." Ask: "What is the sound in the middle? Say it again." After writing: "Touch each letter and read what you wrote. Is it the word?"
note.watch: Have children read their own spelling back; it catches a missing vowel better than you can. Spelling by sound that can be read ("frend") is progress at this age; correct the words that are in the word bank.

1:syllables-split.title: Syllables
1:syllables-split.objective: Children clap the parts of a word, mark each syllable, and write a word with a dash between its syllables.

note.mistake: Children clap once for each sound or each letter, or they stretch a one-syllable word into two claps ("ca-at"). In writing they put the dash anywhere, often after the first letter.
note.words: Say: "Put your hand under your chin. Say the word. Every time your chin drops is a syllable: rab-bit, two." Then: "Every syllable has one vowel sound. Two consonants between the vowels? Split between them: rab-bit, pen-cil." Say words in a robot voice: "pen-cil."
note.watch: Use the chin check with children who clap too many, and have children who clap too few hum the word; the chin hardly moves on sounds like ee (ba-by, bun-ny). On the dash page, check that each part has a vowel letter, and count y as a vowel at the end of a word (pup-py, can-dy); a part with no vowel cannot be a syllable.

1:word-families-syllable-reading.title: Word families
1:word-families-syllable-reading.objective: Children read the words of a word family, find the one that names a picture, and write its beginning before the ending.

note.mistake: Children read the first word of a family and say the rest by rhyming, without looking at the first letter. Or they sound out every word from scratch and never use the ending they just read.
note.words: Say: "These words all end the same: -at. Only the beginning changes. c-at, h-at, m-at." Cover the ending and ask: "What does this one start with?" Then: "If you can read 'cat,' you can read 'flat.'"
note.watch: Point to words out of order and listen. A child who reads them in a row and stumbles when you skip around was reciting; mix the order and add one word from another family.

1:read-and-follow.title: Read and do
1:read-and-follow.objective: Children read a sentence and do exactly what it says: color or circle the pictures it names.

note.mistake: Children read the first words, catch the name of a picture, and color it any color. The small words carry the meaning and are skipped: "two," "red," "not," "last."
note.words: Say: "Read the whole sentence before you pick up a crayon or a pencil. Then tell me: WHAT do you color or circle? HOW MANY? Which COLOR?" Have the child underline the number word and the color word. "Read it again and check your work."
note.watch: The page checks itself: a wrong color or count shows which word was missed. Sit with a child for one sentence and note whether the trouble is reading the words or keeping the sentence in mind.

1:cloze.title: Fill in the missing word
1:cloze.objective: Children read a sentence with a blank and choose the word or the picture that makes sense in it.

note.mistake: Children pick a word that goes with the picture and do not read the sentence to the end, so the word does not fit. Or they take the next unused word from the word bank.
note.words: Say: "Read every word in the word bank first. Now read the sentence and say 'blank' at the empty spot. Try a word: does it make sense? Does it sound right?" Have children read the finished sentence aloud. "Every sentence has to make sense when you read it."
note.watch: Listen to the child read a finished sentence. A sentence that makes no sense and does not bother the child is the real finding; that child is reading words, not meaning.

1:unscramble-sentence.title: Unscramble the sentence
1:unscramble-sentence.objective: Children put mixed-up words in order and write the sentence with a capital letter and an end mark.

note.mistake: Children copy the words in the order they are printed. When they do find the order, they forget the capital letter at the start or the mark at the end.
note.words: Say: "Find the word with the capital letter: it most likely goes first. A name and the word I have a capital too, so check. Find the word with the end mark: it goes last." Then: "Who or what is the sentence about? What happens?" Have children say the sentence aloud before they write it.
note.watch: Have the child read the written sentence aloud. Check three things in order: does it make sense, does it start with a capital, does it end with a mark.

1:question-words.title: Who, what, where
1:question-words.objective: Children choose the question word, who, what, or where, that asks for a part of a sentence, and match questions to answers.

note.mistake: Children choose "what" for everything. "Who" and "where" are mixed up when the answer is a place with a person in it ("at Grandma's").
note.words: Give each word its job: "WHO asks about a person. WHAT asks about a thing or an action. WHERE asks about a place." Ask about a classroom sentence: "Maya reads in the corner. Who reads? What does she do? Where?"
note.watch: Ask a child to make up a question for an answer you give ("in the kitchen"). Making the question shows more than circling does.

1:story-sequencing.title: What happens next?
1:story-sequencing.objective: Children look at the pictures of a story, choose what happens next, and put the sentences of a story in order.

note.mistake: Children choose a picture that shows the same things and not one that follows from what happened. With sentences, they number them in the order printed, or match a sentence to a picture by one word.
note.words: Ask: "What happened first? What changed? So what could happen next, and why?" Use the order words: "first, then, next, last." Have the child tell the whole story in a few sentences after finishing.
note.watch: Ask "Why that one?" A child who answers with a cause ("because the cup fell") is following the story; one who says "because it has the cat" is matching pictures.

1:alphabetical-order.title: ABC order
1:alphabetical-order.objective: Children put words in alphabetical order by their first letter, and by the second letter when two words start the same.

note.mistake: Children order the words by where they think the letter comes in the song and lose track in the middle of the alphabet. When two words start with the same letter, they stop or order them by length.
note.words: Say: "Look only at the first letter. Find each one on the alphabet strip. Which comes first on the strip?" For a tie: "Both start with b. Cover the b. Now look at the next letter."
note.watch: Keep the alphabet strip in sight; the goal is using the order, not reciting it. Check the pairs that start alike: a child who numbers "bed" before "bat" has not moved on to the second letter; cover the first letters and ask again.

1:word-classes.title: Nouns, verbs, and adjectives
1:word-classes.objective: Children sort words into nouns and verbs, and into nouns and adjectives.

note.mistake: Children sort by what a word makes them think of: "party" and "game" go with the verbs because you do something there, and "fast" or "hungry" goes with the verbs because it happens to you. Words that can be both (a walk, to walk) confuse them, and rightly so.
note.words: Give each kind a test sentence: "A noun is a person, place, animal, or thing. Try it here: 'I see the ___.' I see the dog. A verb is something you can do. Try it here: 'I can ___.' I can jump. An adjective tells what something is like. Try it here: 'The dog is very ___.' The dog is very big."
note.watch: Have children use the test aloud for the hard words. If a child argues that "paint" can be both, the child is right; say so and ask for a sentence each way.

1:pronouns.title: He, she, it, they
1:pronouns.objective: Children choose the pronoun that takes the place of a name and write it in a sentence.

note.mistake: Children write the name again in the second sentence, or use "they" only for a crowd and not for two people. They are unsure about "it" for an animal or a thing. Children who are learning English may use "he" for everyone or mix up "he" and "she."
note.words: Say: "We do not say the name over and over. 'Ben has a kite. Ben flies the kite' becomes 'Ben has a kite. HE flies it.'" Ask: "Who is 'he' in this sentence? Point to the name." For two people: "Ben and Mia: they." For a thing: "The kite: it."
note.watch: Have the child read both sentences aloud and tell you who the pronoun means. Children learning English may not have he and she in their home language; give them more spoken practice.

1:opposites.title: Write the opposite
1:opposites.objective: Children find the opposite of a word in a word bank and tell an opposite from a word that means the same.

note.mistake: Children circle the word that means the same, because it is the word that "goes with" the first one. On the word bank page they take a word that is about the same thing and is not the opposite, such as "warm" for "hot."
note.words: Say: "Opposite means as different as can be: hot, cold. Same means nearly alike: big, large." Test a word with "not": "If the door is not open, it is… shut. So open and shut are opposites." Ask: "Is that word the opposite, or does it mean the same?"
note.watch: On the three-word page, a child who circles the same-meaning word knows the words are related and has not sorted out how. Ask for both: "Which one means the same? Which one is the opposite?"

1:shades-of-meaning.title: From a little to a lot
1:shades-of-meaning.objective: Children put three words with nearly the same meaning in order from the weakest to the strongest.

note.mistake: Children treat the three words as meaning exactly the same and number them in the order printed. They know the plain word (big) and are unsure of the strong one (enormous).
note.words: Act the words out or show them with your hands: "Show me cool. Show me cold. Show me freezing." Ask: "Which one is the most? Which is only a little?" Use them in one sentence: "The water is cool… cold… freezing!"
note.watch: Ask which word of a row the child did not know. Ordering three words is easy once the words are known; the lesson is really about learning the strong word.

1:root-words.title: Find the root word
1:root-words.objective: Children name a picture and find the longer word that is built from that word, such as rain in rainy.

note.mistake: Children circle a word that only starts with the same letters as the picture word and has nothing to do with it: "carrot" for the picture of a car, "panda" for the picture of a pan.
note.words: Say: "A root word is the word a longer word is built from, and the meaning stays. Rain, rainy, raining: all about rain." Test it: "Does a carrot have anything to do with a car? No. So 'carrot' is not built from 'car.'"
note.watch: Ask the child what the long word means. If the meaning has the picture word in it (a teacher teaches), the root is right; if not, the letters match by accident.

1:articles.title: A or an: sort the words
1:articles.objective: Children read a word, decide whether a or an belongs in front of it, and write it in the right group.

note.mistake: Children put every word under "a," because "a" is the word they use most, or they stop reading and fill the two groups evenly. A child who sorts correctly by the first letter has the right answers here and will go wrong later on words such as "hour" and "unicorn," where the letter and the sound do not agree.
note.words: Say: "Read the word. Say its first sound. Is it a vowel sound? Then it goes under an." Check by ear: "A egg… an egg. Which one do we say?" Have children read each finished group aloud: "an apple, an egg, an owl."
note.watch: Listen to the child read the finished lists with the article in front. A wrong word stands out at once when it is said aloud; have the child find it by ear, not by rule.

1:synonyms.title: Two words that mean the same thing
1:synonyms.objective: Children look at a picture and circle the two words under it that mean the same and tell about the picture.

note.mistake: Children circle two words that both fit the picture and do not mean the same (big and gray for an elephant), or they circle a word and its opposite, because opposites also belong together.
note.words: Say: "Words that mean the same can trade places. The big dog, the large dog: same picture in your head." Test a pair in one sentence: "The elephant is big. The elephant is large. Same? The elephant is gray. Same?" Call them "words that mean the same," and give the word "synonyms" once.
note.watch: Have the child say both circled words in one sentence about the picture. If the meaning changes from one sentence to the other, the words are not synonyms; have the child keep one word and test it against each of the others.

3:input-output.title: Number machines
3:input-output.objective: Children use the rule printed on a number machine, such as + 7, − 4, or × 5, to fill in the missing numbers going in and coming out.

note.mistake: Children use the rule the same way in every row. When the number that went IN is missing, they apply the rule forward again and do not undo it: on a + 7 machine with 12 coming out they write 19, not 5; on a × 5 machine with 30 coming out they write 150, not 6. Some read a minus rule as plus.
note.words: Have children read the rule aloud first: "This machine adds 7 to every number." For a number coming out (the output): "5 goes in. Add 7. What comes out?" For a number going in (the input): "12 came out. The machine added 7. What went in? Undo it: 12 minus 7." On a times machine: "30 came out. The machine multiplied by 5. What number times 5 makes 30?" Ask: "How can you check? Put your number in and run the machine."
note.watch: Check the rows where the missing number is the one going in; those need the opposite operation. Have the child put the answer back through the machine: if 5 plus 7 gives the 12 that is printed, the row is right.

3:volume-cubes.title: Count the cubes
3:volume-cubes.objective: Children count all the unit cubes in a tower, also the ones they cannot see, and write the total.

note.mistake: Children count only the cubes they can see in the drawing and leave out the hidden ones at the back and underneath. Or they count the square faces they see and get a number that is far too big.
note.words: Build the tower with snap cubes first: "How many can you see from here? Now turn it around and take it apart. Count them all." Say: "Count layer by layer. How many cubes in the bottom layer? In the next one? Add the layers." Ask: "A cube on top must be sitting on something. What is under it?" Give the word: "The number of cubes that fill a shape is its volume."
note.watch: Have each child build one tower from the page with cubes and compare the count with the written answer. A child who counts by layers ("6 and 6 and 6") is ready for volume as layers times the cubes in a layer.

3:fraction-number-line.title: Fractions on a number line
3:fraction-number-line.objective: Children read the fraction that a dot marks on a number line from 0 to 1 by counting the equal spaces.

note.mistake: Children count the tick marks, the ones at 0 and at 1 included, and take that for the bottom number: a line cut into 4 equal spaces has 5 marks and becomes "fifths." Or they count the marks up to the dot, starting with 1 at zero.
note.words: Say: "Count the SPACES between 0 and 1, not the marks. Four equal spaces: each one is one fourth. So the denominator, the bottom number, is 4." Then hop from zero: "One fourth, two fourths, three fourths. The dot is at three fourths." Ask: "Where is zero fourths? Where is four fourths?"
note.watch: Ask a child how they found the bottom number. "I counted the lines" means the marks were counted; fold a paper strip into fourths and lay it under the line to show the four spaces.

3:fraction-of-set.title: A fraction of a group
3:fraction-of-set.objective: Children circle a fraction of a group of pictures, such as one third of 12, and write how many that is.

note.mistake: Children circle as many pictures as the bottom number says: 3 pictures for one third. With a top number above 1 (two thirds), they find one group and stop.
note.words: Say: "The denominator, the bottom number, tells how many equal groups to make. Thirds: make 3 equal groups. One third is ONE of the groups." Link it to division: "12 in 3 equal groups: 4 in each. One third of 12 is 4." For two thirds: "The numerator, the top number, tells how many groups to take. Two of the groups: 4 and 4, that is 8."
note.watch: Check that the groups a child circles are equal before looking at the number. A child who knows 12 ÷ 3 = 4 and still circles 3 pictures has not connected the fraction with the division; have that child deal 12 counters into 3 equal groups first.

K:heavy-light.title: Which is heavier?
K:heavy-light.objective: Children look at two everyday objects and circle the one that is heavier.

note.mistake: Children circle the thing that looks bigger. A big balloon is chosen over a small rock, because to them bigger has always meant more.
note.words: Bring a balloon and a rock, or a big empty box and a small full bottle: "Which is bigger? Which is heavier? Hold one in each hand." Say: "Big is how much room it takes up. Heavy is how hard it pushes down on your hand."
note.watch: Look at the pairs where the smaller thing is the heavier one; those tell you who understands. Let children be the balance: arms out, one thing in each hand, and the heavy side goes down. If two things feel about the same, put them on a pan balance.

2:sentence-boundaries.title: Capital letters and end marks
2:sentence-boundaries.objective: Children rewrite a sentence with its capital letter and its end mark, and split two sentences that ran together.

note.mistake: Children add the period and forget the capital, or the other way around. With two sentences run together, they put the period where they would take a breath, and one of the two "sentences" has no verb.
note.words: Say: "A sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a mark. Both, every time." For run-on sentences: "Read it aloud. Where does the first idea stop? Who is the second sentence about?" Test each part: "Does it tell who or what, and what happens?"
note.watch: Have the child read each of the two new sentences alone. If one of them does not make sense by itself, the break is in the wrong place. Check that the second sentence got its own capital letter.

2:word-classes.title: Nouns, verbs, and adjectives: three bins
2:word-classes.objective: Children sort words into nouns, verbs, and adjectives and write each word in its bin.

note.mistake: Children put a word in a bin by a feeling ("happy" is a verb because you can "be happy"). Words that can be two things (a drink, to drink; a play, to play) are sorted one way with no second thought.
note.words: Give three test sentences: "Noun: can you say 'I see the ___' or 'I have some ___'? Verb: can you say 'I can ___' or 'She ___s every day'? Adjective: can you say 'The thing is very ___'?" For a word that fits two bins: "Use it in a sentence. Now which is it?"
note.watch: Ask for a sentence with any word a child placed in a surprising bin; a good sentence can make the child right. Adjectives are the weakest bin for most children, so check that bin first.

2:plural-nouns.title: More than one: plural nouns
2:plural-nouns.objective: Children write the plural of a noun, with -s, with -es, and for nouns that change, such as mouse and mice.

note.mistake: Children add -s to everything: "foxs," "mouses," "childs." The opposite also happens: after learning the new word, a child marks the plural twice and writes "mices," "feets," or "childrens."
note.words: Say the plural aloud first: "One fox, two foxes. Do you hear the extra beat? Then it needs -es. If the word already ends in e, as in horse, just add s." For the ones that change: "These you have to know: one mouse, two mice; one child, two children; one foot, two feet." Keep a class list of them.
note.watch: Sort a child's errors: -s where -es belongs is a spelling rule to teach; "mouses" is a word to learn by heart. The two need different help.

2:verb-forms.title: Today and yesterday: verb forms
2:verb-forms.objective: Children write the present and the past form of a verb, including be, have, do, and go, and use the right form in a sentence.

note.mistake: Children add -ed to every verb: "goed," "runned," "haved." With "be" they do not see that am, is, are, was, and were are all one verb.
note.words: Use two sentence frames all through: "Today I ___. Yesterday I ___." Say them aloud: "Today I go. Yesterday I went." For be: "Today I am, you are, she is. Yesterday I was, you were, she was." Ask: "Does it sound right?"
note.watch: Listen for the forms children use when they talk; many say "went" and still write "goed" when a page asks for an ending. Have them read their sentence aloud and listen. The ear helps only children who hear these forms every day; for children learning English, or whose home speech uses other forms ("he do," "we was"), teach the forms from a class chart without calling the home form wrong. In the sentences, check has, does, and goes after he, she, or it.

2:pronouns.title: Who does the pronoun stand for?
2:pronouns.objective: Children find the name a pronoun stands for and rewrite a sentence with a pronoun in place of the name.

note.mistake: Children link a pronoun to the nearest name, not to the one it means: in "Sam gave Lily his book," "his" is tied to Lily. When rewriting, they pick the wrong form ("Him went home").
note.words: Ask: "Who is 'she' here? Put the name back in. Does the sentence still say the same thing?" For rewriting: "Is the person doing the action? Then he, she, or they. Is something done to the person? Then him, her, or them. Does something belong to the person? Then his, her, or their."
note.watch: Use the put-the-name-back test on each line a child drew. Read rewritten sentences aloud together; "Him went home" sounds wrong to most children once they hear it.

2:question-words.title: Write the question
2:question-words.objective: Children write a question that asks for a given answer, choosing among who, what, where, when, why, and how.

note.mistake: Children write a statement with a question mark at the end ("The dog is in the yard?"), or they start with the right question word and keep the word order of a statement ("Where the dog is?"). When the sentence has an action verb, they leave out "does" or "did" ("What Maya eats?").
note.words: Say: "The highlighted words are the ANSWER. Which question word asks for a place? A reason? A way of doing it?" Build it aloud: "The dog is in the yard. Where… is the dog?" Point out the switch: "is the dog," not "the dog is." With an action verb: "Maya eats an apple. What DOES Maya eat?"
note.watch: Read a child's question and answer it yourself with the highlighted words. If your answer does not fit the question, the question word is wrong. Check for the question mark last.

2:digraphs.title: Review: find sh in sentences
2:digraphs.objective: Children read sentences, circle every sh, including the ones in the middle and at the end of a word, and count them.

note.mistake: Children find sh at the start of words and miss it in the middle and at the end (fishing, brush). Some circle every s and every h they see, even when the two letters are not side by side.
note.words: Say: "sh is a team: the two letters are side by side and make one sound." Read each sentence aloud slowly and have children raise a hand when they HEAR /sh/. Then: "Now find it with your eyes. Beginning, middle, or end?" Add: "If you hear /sh/ and cannot find sh, as in 'sure,' tell me: that word spells the sound another way."
note.watch: Compare the number in the box with the number of circles. A child who reads silently misses more; have that child whisper the sentence. Check words like "fish" and "washing," where the team is not at the start.

2:spelling-rules.title: Spelling rules: which letters go here?
2:spelling-rules.objective: Children read a spelling rule and choose the right letters for a sound by where it is in the word, for example ck after a short vowel.

note.mistake: Children spell a sound the same way everywhere: "duk" and "bike" both get a plain k. They can say the rule as a sentence and do not check the sound that comes before.
note.words: Read the rule on the page together and turn it into a question to ask each time. For ck and k, for example: "What comes right before the /k/ sound? One short vowel?" Say: "Right after one short vowel, ck: duck, sock. After anything else, just k: milk, book, bike." Have children say the word, then the sound just before /k/, then the spelling.
note.watch: Ask the child why a word got its letters. "Because of the rule" is not enough; the child should name the sound that comes before. Each page practices one rule; mix the rules only after each has been practiced alone.

2:compound-words.title: Compound words
2:compound-words.objective: Children join two words to make a compound word and find where a compound word splits into its two words.

note.mistake: Children split a word wherever they see a small word inside it: "car-pet," "but-ton." In a real compound they cut after the first few letters and not where the second word begins. On the matching page they join two pictures that go together in life (sun and moon) and not two that make a word (sun and flower).
note.words: Say: "A compound word is two whole words stuck together, and both still mean something: rain + coat, a coat for the rain." Test a split: "Is 'car' a word? Is 'pet' a word? Is a carpet a pet in a car? Then it is not a compound."
note.watch: Have the child say both halves and tell what the whole word means with both halves in it ("a brush for teeth"). A split that leaves a half that is not a word shows at once.

2:root-words.title: Root words and word families
2:root-words.objective: Children find the root that three words share and sort words by their root.

note.mistake: Children circle only the letters that are printed the same in all three words, so the root of "baker, baking, baked" becomes "bak." Or they keep a letter that was only added for spelling: the root of "running" becomes "runn."
note.words: Say: "The root is the part that means the same in all three: play, player, playing. What do they all have to do with?" Cover the endings with a finger. For a changed spelling: "Running comes from run; the extra n is there for the spelling. Baking comes from bake; the e was dropped. Write the root the way it is spelled when it stands alone."
note.watch: Ask what the three words have in common in MEANING before the child circles. Then have the child read the root written in the stone: is it a real word by itself? "Bak" and "runn" are not, so the child goes back and repairs the spelling.

2:synonyms.title: Synonyms
2:synonyms.objective: Children choose and match words that mean the same, such as glad and happy.

note.mistake: Children pick a word that often goes with the first word (cold and ice, big and house) and not one that could take its place. On the matching page they join the easy pairs and then link the leftover words without reading them.
note.words: Give the swap test: "Put the new word in the sentence where the old one was. Does the sentence still mean the same?" Try it: "I am glad. I am happy. Same. I am glad. I am sad. Not the same." Use the word "synonym."
note.watch: Note the words nobody knew; those are vocabulary to teach first, because no test finds a synonym for a word a child has never met. Ask a child to use both words of one pair in the same sentence.

2:synonyms~doing-stage.title: More exact words for "said"
2:synonyms~doing-stage.objective: Children read a sentence and choose a more exact word than said, such as whispered, shouted, or asked.

note.mistake: Children take the words in the order they are printed in the bubble, or use one favorite ("shouted") everywhere. They do not look for the clue in the sentence that tells how something was said.
note.words: Ask: "HOW did the person say it? Look for a clue: a question mark, an exclamation point, a word like 'quietly.'" Act it out: "Say it in a whisper. Now shout it. Which word fits what happened?"
note.watch: Have the child read the finished sentence in the voice the new word calls for. If "whispered" comes before a sentence with an exclamation point, the child will hear the clash.

2:read-and-answer.title: Read a story and answer questions
2:read-and-answer.objective: Children read a short story and answer who, what, where, when, and why questions with details from the text.
