note.mistake: Children answer from what they know about the world or from the first sentence they remember, without going back to the story. A wrong answer that uses a word from the story is picked because the word looks familiar.
note.words: Say: "The answer is in the story. Go back and find the sentence that tells you. Put your finger on it." Ask after each answer: "Where does it say that?" For a why question: "Look for 'because,' or for what happened just before."
note.watch: Ask a child to show the sentence that proves one answer. A child who can point to it is reading closely; one who says "I just know" is guessing, even when the answer is right.

2:cloze-context.title: Fill in the story's missing words
2:cloze-context.objective: Children read a whole short story and use what happens in it to choose the word that belongs in each blank.

note.mistake: Children fill the first blank after reading only up to it, and choose a word that fits that one sentence and not the story. A word used wrongly early leaves the wrong word for the last blank.
note.words: Say: "Read the WHOLE story first and say 'blank' at each empty box. What is the story about?" Then: "Try a word. Read on to the next sentence. Does it still make sense?" Add: "Sometimes the clue comes after the blank, so read ahead as well as back."
note.watch: See whether a child reads to the end before writing. Have the finished story read aloud; a word in the wrong blank makes a sentence that sounds odd, and most children catch it by ear.

2:describe-a-picture.title: Write about a picture
2:describe-a-picture.objective: Children write sentences about a picture with sentence starters and a word bank, and then write their own short story about a picture with the word bank only.

note.mistake: Children write a list ("a dog, a ball, a tree") and not sentences, or every sentence begins "I see." Words are copied from the word bank with no capital at the start of the sentence and no period.
note.words: Ask for a whole thought: "Who or what is in the picture? What is it doing? Where?" Say a sentence together before writing it: "The dog runs after the ball." Offer new beginnings: "Next to the tree…", "A girl…", "In the sky…"
note.watch: Count the different sentence beginnings on a child's page. Have the child read the writing aloud and point to each period; a missing verb shows when the sentence is read.

2:retell-with-starters.title: Retell a story: first, next, then, at the end
2:retell-with-starters.objective: Children write what happens in each picture of a story in order, beginning with the time-order word that is given.

note.mistake: Children describe each picture by itself ("There is a cat") and do not tell what HAPPENS or how one picture leads to the next. Some copy the starter word and then begin a new sentence, so the starter is left alone.
note.words: Tell the story aloud before anyone writes: "First… Next… Then… At the end…" Ask at each picture: "What happened here? Why? What changed since the last picture?" Show how the starter joins the sentence: "First, the cat climbs the tree."
note.watch: Have the child read the four parts as one story. It should make sense to someone who cannot see the pictures; if it does not, ask what the listener would need to know.

2:animal-fact-file.title: An animal fact sheet
2:animal-fact-file.objective: Children choose true facts about an animal, such as what it eats, where it lives, and how it moves, and write them on a fact sheet.

note.mistake: Children circle what they know from stories and cartoons and not what is true: honey for the bear, cheese for the mouse. When copying from the word bank, a fact lands in the wrong row: what the animal eats is written under where it lives.
note.words: Say: "A fact is true, and we can check it in a book or by looking." Read the row names first: "What does this row ask for? Food, home, or how it moves?" Ask: "How do you know that? Where could we check?"
note.watch: Ask a child to read one row name and then the fact beside it; a fact in the wrong row sounds wrong at once. Keep a few animal books on hand and let children check one fact each.

2:cursive-writing.title: Cursive letters and connections
2:cursive-writing.objective: Children trace and write rows of connected cursive letters (i, t, u, and w) and connect two letters without lifting the pencil (for schools that teach cursive in Grade 2).

note.mistake: Children lift the pencil after every letter and add the connecting stroke afterward, so the row is print letters with tails. Some stop in the middle of a word to dot the i or cross the t, which breaks the flow.
note.words: Say: "Keep the pencil down until the whole word is written. Then go back: dot the i, cross the t." Name the strokes: "up, down, and out to the next letter." For w: "W ends high, at the middle line, so the next letter starts from up there, not from the bottom line." Write it big in the air first, then on the page.
note.watch: Watch the pencil, not the page: is it lifted inside a word? Check that each connection starts where the letter before it ended and that the letters sit on the line. Right-handed children tilt the paper with its top to the left; left-handed children tilt it with its top to the right, so that the hand stays below the writing.

2:prefixes.title: Prefixes change the meaning
2:prefixes.objective: Children add a prefix such as un-, dis-, re-, or mis- to a word and tell what the new word means.

note.mistake: Children put any prefix on any word ("unhonest," "dishappy"), or they see a prefix in a word that has none: "uncle" and "under" are taken apart. They can build the word and cannot say what it means.
note.words: Give each prefix a meaning to say: "un-, dis-, and in- mean not or the opposite of. re- means again. pre- means before. mis- means wrong or badly." Use it: "Unhappy: not happy. Dishonest: not honest. Incorrect: not correct. Reread: read again. Preheat: heat before. Misspell: spell wrong." Test a doubtful word: "Take off un-. Is 'cle' a word? Then 'uncle' has no prefix."
note.watch: Have the child explain each new word with the prefix's meaning in it. For un-, dis-, and in-, only some pairs exist; children learn those by hearing them, so say the right word back ("dishonest") and give no rule. Watch for words where in- means "in" and not "not" (inside, indoors); tell the child that this in- is a different one.

3:word-fields.title: Words for go and words for look
3:word-fields.objective: Children sort verbs such as stroll, dash, glance, and stare into groups by meaning and tell the close words apart.

note.mistake: Children know "go" and "look" and take the other words for the same thing said in a fancier way. A word they do not know is placed by guess or left out.
note.words: Act each word out: "Show me stroll. Show me dash. Are they both ways to go? What is different?" Then for looking: "Glance at the door. Stare at the door." Ask: "When would you use this word and not the plain one?"
note.watch: Ask a child to use two words from one group in two sentences that show the difference. Note the words nobody could act out; teach those before the page is corrected.

3:person-words.title: The person word: bake, baker
3:person-words.objective: Children make the word for a person from a verb with the ending -er, as in bake and baker, and say what the new word means.

note.mistake: Children add -er without the spelling change: "runer," "bakeer," "swimer." They also take every word that ends in -er for a person word, such as "water" and "finger."
note.words: Say: "A baker is a person who bakes. A runner is a person who runs." Give the two spelling moves: "Bake ends in e: drop the e, then add -er. Baker. Run has one short vowel and one consonant at the end: double the consonant, then add -er. Runner." Test a word: "Is a finger a person who fings?"
note.watch: Have the child say the meaning as "a person who…" for each new word. Check the doubled letters (runner, swimmer) and the dropped e (baker, writer); those are the two places where errors gather.

3:root-words-in-context.title: Choose the right form of the word
3:root-words-in-context.objective: Children choose among four words from one family, such as bake, baker, baking, and baked, the one that fits each sentence.

note.mistake: Children put the words into the blanks in the order they are printed. They choose by meaning alone, which all four words share, and do not listen for what the sentence needs: a person, an action now, or an action that is over.
note.words: Ask what the blank needs: "Is it a person? Something that is happening, after is or are? Something that already happened? Or the plain word, after to, will, or can?" Read the sentence aloud with each word: "Yesterday she… bake? baker? baked. Which one sounds right?" Cross off each word as it is used.
note.watch: Have the child read all four finished sentences aloud. One wrong word forces a second one, so two sentences will sound wrong together; let the child trade the two words.

K:conservation.title: Still the same number
K:conservation.objective: Children count two groups of the same kind of object, one in a row and one spread out, write how many are in each, and decide whether both groups have the same number.

note.mistake: Children say that the spread-out group has more because it takes up more room, and some change their answer when the same objects are pushed together. In the scattered group many skip an object or count one twice.
note.words: Move the counters while the children watch. Ask: "Did I add any? Did I take any away? So how many are there now?" Say: "Moving them does not change how many." For the scattered group say: "Mark each one as you count it."
note.watch: Watch who has to count again from 1 after you have only moved the counters, and who says the number right away. In the scattered group, watch for the child who counts without marking.

K:one-more-one-less.title: One more, one less
K:one-more-one-less.objective: Children count a group of up to 9 pictures, draw one more or cross one out as the label says, and write how many there are now.

note.mistake: Children count the whole group again from 1 after one more is added, when the next counting number is the answer. On the page with both labels some draw one more on every task and do not look at "1 less".
note.words: Ask: "You counted 6. One more comes. Which number comes right after 6?" and "One goes away. Which number comes just before 6?" Have children say the whole sentence: "One more than 6 is 7."
note.watch: Watch who names the new number without counting again. A child who recounts every time needs more turns with real counters on a ten-frame: put one on, say the next number, take it off, say the number before.

K:compare-groups#which-number-is-greater.title: Which number is greater?
K:compare-groups#which-number-is-greater.objective: Children compare two written numbers from 1 to 10 and color the greater one.

note.mistake: With no pictures to count, some children choose the number that is printed on the right, or the one they like. Others mix up "greater" with "comes first" when they count.
note.words: Ask: "Which of the two numbers do you say later when you count? That one is greater." Say both sentences: "7 is greater than 5. 5 is less than 7." Have children build both numbers as cube towers and say which tower is taller.
note.watch: Watch the pairs that are close together, such as 7 and 8 or 5 and 6. A child who is sure about 2 and 8 but guesses on 7 and 8 needs the number line or the cube towers for a while longer.

K:numeral-formation#write-11-to-20.title: Write the numbers 11 to 20
K:numeral-formation#write-11-to-20.objective: Children trace the numbers 11 to 20 with the digits in the right order, starting each digit at the dot and following the arrows. Then they write each number once on their own on a whiteboard.

note.mistake: Children write the digits in the order they hear them: 71 for seventeen and 41 for fourteen. Some start a digit at the bottom, and many turn the 2, 3, 5, or 7 around inside a teen number.
note.words: Say: "Every number from 11 to 19 starts with a 1. The 1 stands for one ten." Ask: "Which digit do you write first?" For seventeen say: "I hear seven first, but I write the 1 first."
note.watch: Watch the order in which a child writes the two digits, not only how the finished number looks. A child who writes the second digit first will write 71 for 17 as soon as the tracing lines are gone.

K:count-on.title: Count on from a number
K:count-on.objective: Children start at the number printed on a closed box, count on over the pictures beside it, and write how many there are in all, with totals up to 10.

note.mistake: Children start again at 1 and try to count things they cannot see inside the box. Others say the number on the box a second time for the first picture beside it and end one short.
note.words: Tap the box and stretch out its number: "Siiix." Then point to each picture beside it: "seven, eight." Ask: "Do we need to count what is in the box? What does the number on it tell us?"
note.watch: Listen to the first word a child says. A child who whispers "1, 2, 3" up to the number on the box is still counting all. Practice with a real closed bag that has its number written on it.

K:take-away.title: Take away: how many are left?
K:take-away.objective: Children look at a ten-frame on which some dots are crossed out, count the dots that are left, and finish the subtraction sentence, such as 7 − 2 = 5.

note.mistake: Children count all the dots, crossed out or not, and write the starting number again. Others count the crossed-out dots and write how many were taken away, not how many are left.
note.words: Say: "7 dots. 2 are crossed out; they are gone. Count the ones that are still there." Read the sentence together: "7 take away 2 is 5." Ask: "Which number tells how many are left?"
note.watch: Watch which dots a child touches while counting. With real counters on a paper ten-frame, have the child slide the counters that are taken away off the frame so that only the ones that are left stay on it.

1:word-problems#adding-stories-within-10.title: Adding stories: some more come
1:word-problems#adding-stories-within-10.objective: Children listen to a story in which some more come, use the picture of the two groups, and write how many there are in all, with totals up to 10.

note.mistake: Children write one of the two numbers they heard, most often the last one, or count only the second group in the picture. Some cannot retell what happened in the story.
note.words: Read each story aloud twice. Ask: "Who can retell the story? What happened first? What happened then?" Before anyone counts, ask: "Will there be more now, or fewer?" Then say: "Show it with your counters."
note.watch: Watch who can act out the story with counters before writing. A child who counts the pictures correctly but cannot say what the answer tells ("7 cucumbers in all") has counted, not solved the story.

1:word-problems#take-away-stories-within.title: Take-away stories: some go away
1:word-problems#take-away-stories-within.objective: Children listen to a story in which some go away, use the picture in which the ones that go away are crossed out, and write how many are left. The starting number is 10 or less.

note.mistake: Children add the two numbers because every story so far was an adding story. Others count every picture, the crossed-out ones too, and write the starting number.
note.words: Ask: "Did some come, or did some go away? Will there be more or fewer than at the start?" Say: "The crossed-out ones are gone." Have children tell the ending in a sentence: "2 plates are left."
note.watch: Tell one adding story in the middle of the lesson and watch who notices. A child who takes away every time is following the page, not the story.

K:number-bonds-k#take-apart-8-and-9.title: Take apart 8 and 9
K:number-bonds-k#take-apart-8-and-9.objective: Children find the missing part of a number bond when the whole is 8 or 9, and name the two parts that make the whole.

note.mistake: Children write the whole again in the empty circle, or they add the whole and the part they can see. Some know one pair for 8 and think it is the only one.
note.words: Give each child 8 two-color counters to shake and spill. Ask: "How many red? How many yellow? How many in all?" Say: "8 is 5 and 3. 8 is also 6 and 2." Ask: "Is there another way?"
note.watch: Watch who finds the missing part by counting up from the part they see and who still builds the whole with counters. Both are fine at this point; note the child who has no way to start.

1:make-10#how-many-more-to-make-10.title: How many more to make 10?
1:make-10#how-many-more-to-make-10.objective: Children look at a ten-frame with some dots, find how many more make 10, and write the missing number in a sentence such as 6 + 4 = 10.

note.mistake: Children count the dots they see and write that number in the box, when the box asks for the empty squares. On the page with the cup some write 10 again for the ones that are hiding.
note.words: Point to the empty squares: "These are still missing. How many more until the frame is full?" Say: "6 and 4 more make 10." Ask: "How do you know without counting every dot again?"
note.watch: Watch who counts the empty squares one by one and who sees them at a glance (a full row is 5). When the frame is already full, ask what "no more" looks like and which number says it.

K:number-bonds-k#partners-of-10.title: Partners of 10
K:number-bonds-k#partners-of-10.objective: Children find the partner that makes 10 with a given number in a number bond, and say the pair, such as 8 and 2.

note.mistake: Children count on with their fingers and land one off, because they also count the number they start from. Others give the partner of a pair they remember, such as 5, for every number.
note.words: Slide beads on a string of ten: "8 on this side. How many on the other side?" Say it both ways: "8 and 2 make 10. 2 and 8 make 10." Ask: "If you know the partner of 8, what is the partner of 2?"
note.watch: Listen for who knows the turned-around pair at once. A child who works out 2 and 8 again from the start has not yet seen that it is the same pair.

1:true-false-equations.title: True or false?
1:true-false-equations.objective: Children decide whether an addition or subtraction equation within 20 is true or false, including equations that begin with the single number, such as 16 = 13 + 3.

note.mistake: Children read the equal sign as "the answer comes next" and mark 16 = 13 + 3 false because it looks backwards. Others mark an equation true as soon as they recognize the numbers of a fact they know.
note.words: Read the equal sign as "is the same as": "16 is the same as 13 plus 3. Is that true?" Ask: "What is on this side? What is on that side? Are they the same amount?" Have children fix one false equation aloud.
note.watch: Watch the equations that begin with the single number. A child who gets the usual form right and misses those does not need more facts; the child needs the Number Balance, where both sides have to weigh the same.

1:near-doubles.title: Near doubles
1:near-doubles.objective: Children find a sum such as 6 + 7 by using a double and one more (6 + 6 + 1), with sums within 20.

note.mistake: Children do not see the double inside the problem and count on by ones. Others double the larger number and still add one more, so 6 + 7 becomes 15.
note.words: Ask: "Which double is hiding in 6 + 7? How much more is 7 than 6?" Say: "6 + 6 is 12, and one more is 13." Have children say the helping double before they write anything.
note.watch: Watch who writes the sum first and fills in the middle afterward. That child may know the fact, which is fine, but should still be able to say which double helps.

1:fluency-within-20#make-ten-to-add.title: Make ten to add
1:fluency-within-20#make-ten-to-add.objective: Children add a number to 6, 7, 8, or 9 by jumping to ten first and then jumping the rest on a number line, and write the steps, such as 8 + 5 = 8 + 2 + 3 = 13.

note.mistake: Children count on by ones from the first number and never stop at ten. Others split the second number into two parts that do not land on ten, such as 8 + 5 = 8 + 3 + 2.
note.words: Ask: "How many more does 8 need to reach ten? What is left of the 5?" Say: "First to ten, then the rest." Show it on the rekenrek: fill the top row first, then push the rest onto the second row.
note.watch: Watch the first jump: it has to land on ten. A child who draws one long hop straight to the answer has probably counted on by ones and needs more practice with the partners of 10.

1:time-read#match-the-clocks.title: Match the clocks
1:time-read#match-the-clocks.objective: Children read times to the hour and half hour on analog clocks and draw a line from each clock to the digital time that matches.

note.mistake: At half past, children read the hour that the short hand is moving toward and match half past 8 to 9:30. Some look only at the long hand and pair any clock that points to the 6 with any time that ends in 30.
note.words: Ask: "Where is the short hand? Has it reached the 9 yet?" Say: "At half past 8 the short hand is halfway between 8 and 9. It is still 8-something: 8:30." Have children read each matched pair aloud.
note.watch: Watch the two clocks that share an hour, such as 12:00 and 12:30. A child who mixes them up is reading only one of the two hands.

2:equal-shares-shapes#equal-shares-halve.title: Equal shares: fair or not?
2:equal-shares-shapes#equal-shares-halve.objective: Children decide whether a circle or a rectangle is cut into equal shares and circle the shapes that are. With the teacher they name two equal shares halves and four equal shares fourths.

note.mistake: Children count the parts and call any shape with two parts "halves," even when one part is much bigger. Others think that four small pieces are more than two big ones without looking at the whole.
note.words: Ask: "Are the shares the same size? Would it be fair if you got this piece and I got that one?" Say: "Two equal shares are halves. Four equal shares are fourths, or quarters." Several shapes on the page are cut into three equal parts. They are cut fairly too, so children circle them; the name, thirds, comes in Grade 2.
note.watch: Watch the rectangles that are cut into strips of different widths. A child who circles them is counting parts, not comparing sizes; let the child fold a paper strip and lay the parts on top of each other.

2:bundle-ten-ones#ten-tens-make-one-hund.title: Ten tens make one hundred
2:bundle-ten-ones#ten-tens-make-one-hund.objective: Children count the blocks in a picture that has more than nine tens rods, trade ten rods for one hundred, and write the number, such as 12 tens and 5 ones = 125.

note.mistake: Children write what they count, digit by digit: 12 tens and 5 ones becomes 1,205, or 17. Others count the rods by ones and lose track after nine.
note.words: Ask: "How many tens do you see? Can we make a hundred? How many tens are left over?" Say: "Ten tens are the same as one hundred." Have children circle ten rods before they write.
note.watch: Watch who circles ten rods first and who writes the count of rods straight into the number. The second child needs to trade real rods for a hundred flat, or to see the trade on The Exchange Machine.

2:expanded-form-digit-value#expanded-for.title: Expanded form with a zero
2:expanded-form-digit-value#expanded-for.objective: Children put the parts of a three-digit number together and break a number into hundreds, tens, and ones, also when the parts are out of order or a place is empty, such as 50 + 600 = 650 and 900 + 30 = 930.

note.mistake: Children write the parts in the order they are printed: 7 + 500 + 80 becomes 7,580 or 758. With an empty place they push the digits together, so 900 + 30 becomes 93.
note.words: Ask: "Which part is the hundreds? Which place has nothing in it?" Say: "Zero holds the place. 900 + 30 has no ones, so we write a 0 in the ones place." Have children say the name of the number before they write it.
note.watch: Watch the tasks with only two parts. A child who writes 65 for 50 + 600 is reading digits, not values; build the number on the Place Value Lab and keep the empty column in view.

1:open-number-line.title: Jumps on an open number line
1:open-number-line.objective: Children add and subtract two-digit numbers within 100 on an open number line: they mark the starting number, draw their jumps, and write the answer.

note.mistake: Children jump the wrong way when they subtract, or they draw many jumps of one and lose count. Some write the size of the last jump as the answer, not the number they land on.
note.words: Ask: "Where do you start? Are you going forward or back? How big is your first jump?" Say: "Jump the tens first, then the ones," or "Jump to the next ten, then the rest." Have two children show two different ways to solve the same problem.
note.watch: Watch whether a child writes the landing number under every jump. A line with jumps and no landing numbers cannot be checked, by the child or by you.

3:column-regrouping#add-three-digit-numb.title: Add three-digit numbers and make a new ten or hundred
3:column-regrouping#add-three-digit-numb.objective: Children add two three-digit numbers in columns when the ones make a new ten or the tens make a new hundred, and write the small 1 they carry above the next place.

note.mistake: Children write both digits of a sum under one column, so 261 + 285 becomes 4,146. Others carry every time out of habit, or forget to add the 1 they carried.
note.words: Ask at each column: "How many altogether? Is that ten or more? What do we trade?" Say: "14 tens are 1 hundred and 4 tens. The hundred moves to the hundreds column." Have children estimate first: "About 500, or about 5,000?"
note.watch: Watch the column in which no trade is needed. A child who writes a carried 1 there is following a routine without looking at the sum of the column.

3:column-regrouping#subtract-across-a-ze.title: Subtract across zeros
3:column-regrouping#subtract-across-a-ze.objective: Children subtract in columns from a multiple of 100, such as 500 − 231, by trading one hundred for ten tens and then one ten for ten ones.

note.mistake: Children subtract the smaller digit from the larger one in every column, so 500 − 231 becomes 331. Others cross out the 5 and write 10 above both zeros, as if one hundred gave ten tens and ten ones at the same time.
note.words: Ask: "Can you take 1 one from 0 ones? Where can you get ones? Are there any tens to trade?" Say: "Trade one hundred for ten tens. Then trade one ten for ten ones. Now 500 is 4 hundreds, 9 tens, and 10 ones." Keep the blocks on the tables for this lesson.
note.watch: Watch what a child writes above the tens place: it has to end up as 9, not 10. Have the child check one answer by adding it to the number that was taken away.

1:coins#count-mixed-coins.title: Count mixed coins
1:coins#count-mixed-coins.objective: Children count the coins in a purse (quarters, dimes, nickels, and pennies), starting with the coins that are worth the most, and write the total in cents.

note.mistake: Children count how many coins there are, not what they are worth. Others keep counting by the old step when the coin changes: 25, 50, 75, 100 for two quarters, a dime, and a nickel.
note.words: Say: "Start with the coins that are worth the most." Count aloud and stop at each change: "25, 50 ... now a dime: 60 ... now a nickel: 65 ... now a penny: 66." Ask: "What are you counting by now?"
note.watch: Watch the moment the kind of coin changes. Have a child who slips there write the running total under each coin: 25, 50, 60, 65, 66. The coins on the page show their value as a number; use real or plastic coins as well, so that children also learn to tell the coins apart.

1:bar-graphs#make-a-graph-from-counts.title: Make a graph from counts
1:bar-graphs#make-a-graph-from-counts.objective: Children read the counts for four groups and color one box in the graph for each one. Then, with the teacher, they compare the rows of the finished graph: how many more, how many fewer, how many in all.

note.mistake: Children leave a gap or start coloring in the middle of a row, so that a row with fewer boxes reaches farther than a row with more. Others stop coloring when the row looks long enough and do not count.
note.words: Say: "Start next to the picture and color with no gaps." When the graph is done, ask: "Which row is the longest? How many more are in this row than in that one? How many in all?" Have children write an equation for one answer.
note.watch: Watch how a child finds "how many more": by counting the extra boxes, or by subtracting. Both work. A child who answers with the larger count has read one row and has not compared two.

3:times-tables#the-facts-we-still-need.title: The facts we still need
3:times-tables#the-facts-we-still-need.objective: Children fill in a multiplication chart up to 10 × 10, starting with the rows and columns they already know (1, 2, 5, and 10), and list the facts that are left to learn.

note.mistake: Children fill in the chart row by row by skip-counting from the start of each row, which takes the whole lesson and does not show them which facts they already know. Others do not see that 6 × 7 and 7 × 6 are the same fact and count both as unknown.
note.words: Say: "Fill in what you own first: the 1s, 2s, 5s, and 10s, across and down." Ask: "If you know 3 × 5, where is 5 × 3?" Then: "Circle the boxes that are still empty. Those are the facts we still need." Every product you know gives you division facts too: if 6 × 7 = 42, then 42 ÷ 7 = 6.
note.watch: Watch who uses a turn-around fact to fill a box and who starts counting again. Keep each child's list of the facts still needed; it is the practice plan for the next weeks.

K:measurable-attributes.title: What can we measure?
K:measurable-attributes.objective: Children hold a real object, such as a book, a cup, or a block, and say what can be measured about it: how long it is, how heavy it is, or how much it holds.

note.mistake: Children name a color or what the object is used for ("It is red. You drink from it.") and not something that can be measured. Many use "big" for everything, whether the object is long, tall, heavy, or holds a lot.
note.words: Ask: "What could we find out about this cup with a ruler? With a scale? With water?" Say: "We can measure how tall it is, how heavy it is, and how much it holds." Trade "big" for the exact word: "Is it long, tall, or heavy?"
note.watch: Listen for children who name two different things to measure about one object. A child who can only say "big" needs two objects to hold: one that is long and light, and one that is short and heavy.

K:measurable-attributes.routine: Start at the length bench of the Measurement Bench. The class says what is being measured there (how long the object is) and what else could be measured about that object (how heavy it is, how much it holds). Then sit in a circle with a basket of real objects. Each pair takes one object and tells two things about it that can be measured: "We can measure how long it is. We can measure how heavy it is." On the second day each pair takes a new object from the basket and tells again what can be measured about it. This lesson has no worksheet.

K:one-to-one#touch-and-count.title: Touch and count
K:one-to-one#touch-and-count.objective: Children touch and move 1 to 10 real counters one at a time into a ten-frame and say exactly one number for each counter.

note.mistake: Children say the number words faster than they move the counters, so the count runs ahead of the hand. Others count a counter twice or skip one, and some keep counting after the cup is empty.
note.words: Say: "One touch, one number." Count slowly together: "Slide ... one. Slide ... two." Ask: "How many did you put in? How do you know you counted every one?"
note.watch: Watch the hand and listen to the voice at the same time. A child whose last number word lands on the last counter, and who can say "there are 7" without counting again, is ready to write how many.

K:one-to-one#touch-and-count.routine: Model it first on the Ten Frame tool while the class counts along. Then each child gets a cup with 1 to 10 counters and a ten-frame: two rows of five boxes that you draw on paper, or an egg carton cut down to ten cups. The child slides one counter into a box for each number said, fills the top row first, and stops when the cup is empty. Partners watch each other count. This lesson has no worksheet.

2:explain-strategies.title: Why does it work?
2:explain-strategies.objective: Children explain with blocks or a drawing why a way of adding or subtracting within 100 works, and compare two worked ways for the same problem, such as 38 + 25.

note.mistake: Children retell the steps ("I carried the 1") and cannot say what the 1 stands for. Others think that two different ways must give two different answers, or that only the way they learned first is right.
note.words: Ask: "What did this child do first? What happened to the 8 ones and the 5 ones?" Say: "8 ones and 5 ones are 13 ones: 1 new ten and 3 ones." Ask: "Why do both ways give 63?"
note.watch: Listen for place-value words: "3 tens and 2 tens," "I made a new ten." A child who can explain a classmate's way, not only their own, has understood why it works.

2:explain-strategies.routine: Run the lesson as a number talk. Write one problem on the board with two children's ways worked out side by side. For 38 + 25: add tens and ones separately (30 + 20 = 50, 8 + 5 = 13, 50 + 13 = 63) and jump to the next ten (38 + 2 = 40, 40 + 23 = 63). On the second day, for 63 − 28: take away the tens, then the ones (63 − 20 = 43, 43 − 8 = 35) and count up from 28 (28 + 2 = 30, 30 + 33 = 63, so 2 + 33 = 35). Pairs say what each child did and why both ways give the same answer. Then they show 38 + 25 with blocks on the Place Value Lab and 63 − 28 with real blocks. This lesson has no worksheet.

2:estimate-lengths.title: Estimate, then measure
2:estimate-lengths.objective: Children estimate lengths in inches, feet, centimeters, and meters with benchmarks they know, then measure and compare the estimate with the measurement.

note.mistake: Children give an estimate with no unit ("about 10") or change the estimate after they measure so that it looks right. Many guess wildly because they have no picture of an inch or a meter in their heads.
note.words: Ask: "How many times does the tip of your thumb fit along the pencil? So about how many inches long is it?" Say: "An estimate is a smart guess with a unit. It does not have to be exact; it has to be close." Ask: "Was your estimate too long or too short?"
note.watch: Watch the second and third estimates. A child who uses the first measurement to make the next estimate better is estimating; a child whose estimates stay far off needs the benchmarks again.

2:estimate-lengths.routine: Teach four benchmarks first: your little finger is about 1 centimeter wide, your thumb from the tip to the first knuckle is about 1 inch long, a 12-inch ruler is 1 foot long, and a door is about 1 meter wide. Show an inch and a centimeter on the Ruler tool so the class sees how different they are. On the first day pairs estimate in inches or feet, on the second day in centimeters or meters: a pencil, the desk, a bookshelf, and the rug. They estimate first, then measure with a ruler, a yardstick, or a meter stick, and write three things for each, always with the unit: my estimate, my measurement, how far off. This lesson has no worksheet; the children draw three columns on plain paper.

K:teen-numbers#ten-and-some-more.title: Ten and some more
K:teen-numbers#ten-and-some-more.objective: Children count a group of 11 to 19 objects, circle ten of them, and write the number as ten and some more ones, such as 10 + 4 = 14.

note.mistake: After they circle ten, many children count the whole group again from 1. Some circle nine or eleven because they do not use the columns of five. Children who hear "ten and four" sometimes write 104 for 14.
note.words: Say: "Two full columns are ten. Circle them." Ask: "How many are outside your circle?" Then count on together: "Ten, and then 11, 12, 13, 14." Have children say the whole sentence: "14 is ten and four more."
note.watch: Watch who starts again at 1 and who counts on from ten. Check each child's circle on the first problem: a circle around nine or eleven makes the number of extra ones wrong.

K:teen-numbers.title: Teen numbers on two ten-frames
K:teen-numbers.objective: Children count the counters on two ten-frames, one full and one with 1 to 9 counters, write the number, and finish the number sentence, such as 13 = 10 + 3.

note.mistake: Children count every counter in the full frame one by one. When they write, some reverse the digits (31 for 13), because in "thirteen" they hear the three first. Eleven and twelve give no hint of the ten in their names.
note.words: Ask: "Is the first frame full? Then you know it is ten. You do not have to count it." Say: "Ten and three more is thirteen. The 1 is the full frame, the 3 is the other frame." For 11 and 12 say: "Eleven is ten and one. Twelve is ten and two."
note.watch: Watch who taps the full frame counter by counter. Look at the written numbers for reversed digits, most often in 13 to 19, where the ones are spoken first.

1:hundreds-chart#count-to-100.title: Count to 100 on the hundreds chart
1:hundreds-chart#count-to-100.objective: Children count aloud to 100, point to each number on a hundreds chart as they say it, and write the numbers that are missing on the chart.

note.mistake: Children stall at the end of a decade: after 29 they stop or say "twenty-ten." To find a missing number, some start again at 1. In the last rows, digits get reversed (17 for 71).
note.words: At the end of a row ask: "29. Which number starts the next row?" For an empty box say: "Look at the number before the box and the number after it." Count from 21 to 29 together and ask: "Which word did we say every time?"
note.watch: Listen at 29, 39, 49, and so on: that is where the count breaks. Watch who uses the neighbors of an empty box and who counts from the top of the chart every time. Reversed digits in a box are a writing slip at this age, not a counting error.

1:skip-counting#count-by-tens-to-100.title: Count by tens to 100
1:skip-counting#count-by-tens-to-100.objective: Children count aloud by tens to 100, go on from any ten, and write the tens that are missing in rows that count by tens.

note.mistake: Children mix up the -teen and the -ty numbers when they speak and write: 13 for 30, 14 for 40. On a row that starts at 20 or 30, some begin again at 10. After ninety, a few say "tenty."
note.words: Fill real cups with ten beans each and count the cups all the way: "ten, twenty, thirty," on to one hundred. Say: "Thirty ends in -ty: three tens. Thirteen ends in -teen: ten and three." For a row that starts at 20 ask: "Twenty. What is ten more?" One row starts at 0. Say: "Zero means no cups yet. Then comes ten."
note.watch: Look at how 30, 40 and 50 are written: a 13 in the place of 30 shows the mix-up. Watch who can go on from 20 or 30 and who has to start at 10 every time.

1:mental-math-to-100.title: Add tens to a number
1:mental-math-to-100.objective: Children add tens to a two-digit number in their heads, such as 34 + 20, with sums up to 99, and say that only the tens digit changes.

note.mistake: Children add the tens to the ones: 34 + 20 = 36. Others count on by ones twenty times and lose track. When the first number is small, such as 12 + 50, some write 125 or add the 5 to the 2 and get 17.
note.words: Ask: "How many tens are in 34? Three. Add two more tens. How many tens now? And the ones?" Count by tens from the number: "34, 44, 54." In the Number Hotel, take the elevator: it goes up one corridor for every ten, and you stay at the same door. Say: "Only the tens change."
note.watch: Watch who counts by ones and who changes the ones digit. A child who knows 30 + 20 but not 34 + 20 needs to build the number with rods and cubes a few more times and add whole rods.

1:mental-math-to-100#add-ones-to-a-two-d.title: Add ones to a two-digit number
1:mental-math-to-100#add-ones-to-a-two-d.objective: Children add a one-digit number to a two-digit number when the ones stay under ten, such as 32 + 5, and say that the tens do not change.

note.mistake: Children count on by ones on their fingers for every problem, when 2 + 5 already tells them the answer. Some add the single digit to the tens: 32 + 5 = 82. A big first number, such as 85 + 4, makes children unsure of a fact they know.
note.words: Say: "Look at the ones: 2 and 5. What is 2 + 5? So 32 + 5 is thirty-seven." Show the small fact next to the big one: "3 + 4 = 7, so 23 + 4 = 27 and 53 + 4 = 57." Ask: "Did the tens change? Why not?"
note.watch: Watch who uses the small fact and who counts on from the big number. A child who has to count 3 + 4 on fingers needs the facts within 10 first; the two-digit numbers are not the problem.

1:mental-math-to-100#add-ones-and-make-a.title: Add ones and make a new ten
1:mental-math-to-100#add-ones-and-make-a.objective: Children add a one-digit number to a two-digit number when the ones make a new ten, such as 27 + 5: they jump to the next ten on the number line first, then jump the rest, and write the steps, 27 + 3 + 2 = 32.

note.mistake: Children keep the old ten: 27 + 5 = 22. Others write the whole 12 after the 2 and get 212. Some reach 30 and then add the whole 5 again, or split the 5 into two parts that do not land on the ten.
note.words: Ask: "Which ten comes after 27? How far is it to 30? Three." Then: "You have 5 to add and you used 3. How many are left? 30 and 2 more." Have children check: "Do your two jumps make 5 together?"
note.watch: Watch how each child gets to the next ten. A child who counts up to it by ones needs more practice with the pairs that make 10 before this page. Check that the two jumps in the boxes add up to the number being added.

2:add-with-blocks#add-two-two-digit-numb.title: Add two two-digit numbers: tens with tens, ones with ones
2:add-with-blocks#add-two-two-digit-numb.objective: Children add two two-digit numbers shown as rods and cubes when no new ten is made, such as 34 + 25: they add the tens, then the ones, and write the sum up to 99.

note.mistake: Children count each rod as one, so 34 + 25 becomes 3 + 4 + 2 + 5 = 14. Others count the rods one cube at a time and lose the count. When they write the sum, some put the ones first (95 for 59).
note.words: Say: "Rods first. Count them by tens: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50. Now the cubes: 4 and 5 is 9." Then: "5 tens and 9 ones. What number is that?" Give the rule in the children's words: "Tens with tens, ones with ones."
note.watch: Watch who counts a rod as one and who reverses the digits of the sum. Before a child writes, ask how many tens and how many ones there are in all: a child who can say "5 tens and 9 ones, 59" without recounting is ready for adding without blocks.

K:number-bonds-k#take-apart-6-and-7.title: Take apart 6 and 7
K:number-bonds-k#take-apart-6-and-7.objective: Children break a train of 6 or 7 cubes into two parts in different ways, color each way on a strip of squares, and write it as two numbers that make 6 or 7, such as 4 + 2 = 6.

note.mistake: Many children find one way and then color the same way again on the next strip. Some count 4 + 2 and 2 + 4 as the same and stop early; on this page they are two different strips. A few leave one color out and write 6 + 0, which the page does not ask for.
note.words: Give each child a train of six cubes. Say: "Break it into two parts. How many here? How many there?" Then: "Put it back. Can you break it in a different place?" On the page say: "Color the part in one hand red and the part in the other hand blue. Write the red number, then the blue number."
note.watch: Watch who works in order (1 and 5, 2 and 4, 3 and 3) and who jumps around: both are fine, but the child who works in order can tell you when no way is left. Check that the two numbers match the squares the child colored. The easier page gives the two numbers to color; the harder page has strips of 7, so give it to every child once the ways to make 6 are found.

K:teen-numbers#build-and-draw-a-teen-num.title: Build and draw a teen number
K:teen-numbers#build-and-draw-a-teen-num.objective: Children read a written number from 11 to 20, build it with ten cubes on a stick and loose cubes, and draw it on two ten-frames with the first frame full.

note.mistake: Children spread the dots over both frames and leave gaps in the first one, so the ten cannot be seen. Some read 15 as "fifty" and fill both frames. For 20 some stop at ten because the first frame is full.
note.words: Say: "Read the number. Build it: one stick of ten and some more." Then: "Draw the ten first. Fill the first frame, every box." Ask: "How many more do you need? Draw them in the second frame, starting at the top left."
note.watch: Watch whether the child fills the first frame without counting to the number each time. Ask one child at a time: "How do you know this is 14 without counting every dot?" The answer you hope for names the full frame as ten.

K:teen-numbers#ten-and-how-many-more.title: Ten and how many more?
K:teen-numbers#ten-and-how-many-more.objective: Children take 11 to 19 cubes apart into a stick of ten and the rest, and write the missing part in a number bond that has the teen number as the whole and 10 as one part.

note.mistake: Children add the two numbers they see (17 and 10) and write 27 in the empty circle. Others write the whole number again. In a number such as 17 many do not yet see that the 1 stands for the ten.
note.words: Point to the top circle: "This is all of them, 17." Point to the 10: "This part is the stick of ten." Ask: "How many are not on the stick?" Let children check with cubes: snap ten together, count the rest, and say: "17 is ten and seven more."
note.watch: Watch who needs the cubes for every bond and who answers from the number itself (the 7 in 17). On level 3 the ten or the whole can be the empty circle: see whether the child still knows which circle is the whole.

1:hundreds-chart#count-to-50.title: Count to 50
1:hundreds-chart#count-to-50.objective: Children count aloud to 50 by ones, touch each box of a number chart from 1 to 50, and write the numbers that are missing.

note.mistake: The hard places are the turns to a new ten: after 29 many children say "twenty-ten" or jump to 40. When they write, some reverse the digits (12 for 21), most often in the teens, where the ones are said first ("seventeen" written as 71).
note.words: Count together and touch each box. Stop before an empty box: "What did we just say? What comes next?" At the end of a row say: "The row is full. A new ten starts." Show that every number in a column ends with the same digit.
note.watch: Listen to each child count from 25 to 42 alone: this is where the count breaks. On the page, look first at the empty boxes at the start or the end of a row (such as 21), and at whether the child uses the box above to find the number.

K:count-forward-missing#start-at-any-num.title: Start at any number and count on
K:count-forward-missing#start-at-any-num.objective: Children start at a number that is not 1, count on aloud without going back to 1, and write the missing numbers on a number strip.

note.mistake: Many children can only find what comes after 36 by counting from 1, or from 30. At a turn to a new ten (39, 40) they stop or say the wrong ten. Some write the same number as the box before.
note.words: Say a start number and count on together for five numbers: "36. Keep going: 37, 38, 39, 40." Ask: "Do you need to go back to 1? No. Say the number in the box, then the next one." When the tens change, say: "After 39 comes a new ten: 40."
note.watch: Watch who whispers from 1 before writing. Check the strips that cross into a new ten first: a child who cannot write the new ten (39, then 40) needs the number chart beside the page for a few more days.

1:tens-and-ones#teen-numbers-one-ten-and.title: Teen numbers: one ten and some ones
1:tens-and-ones#teen-numbers-one-ten-and.objective: Children build the numbers 11 to 19 with one ten-rod and loose cubes and write them as one ten and some ones.

note.mistake: Children count the ten-rod as one more cube and write 6 for a rod and five cubes. Others count every unit of the rod one by one. When they write, some put the ones first (51 for 15).
note.words: Hold up a rod: "This is one ten. Ten cubes are stuck together, so I do not count them again." Say: "One ten and five ones is fifteen." Have children say it for each picture, then write how many ones and the number.
note.watch: Watch whether the child counts on from ten (10, 11, 12 …) or starts at 1 on the rod. Look at the written numbers for reversed digits, and ask: "Which digit tells you about the rod?"

1:tens-and-ones#count-the-tens.title: Count the tens: 10 to 90
1:tens-and-ones#count-the-tens.objective: Children count 1 to 9 ten-rods, say how many tens there are with no ones left over, and write the number from 10 to 90.

note.mistake: Children write the number of rods as the number (4 for four rods) and leave the zero out. Some count by ones along the rods and lose their place. The names "thirty" and "fifty" do not sound like three tens and five tens.
note.words: Count the rods two ways: "1, 2, 3, 4 tens" and "10, 20, 30, 40." Say: "Four tens and no ones is forty. The 0 says: no ones." Link the names: "Six tens: sixty. Three tens: thirty. Five tens: fifty."
note.watch: Watch whether the child counts by tens or by ones. Check the two boxes of each row: the first holds how many tens, the second the number. A child who writes 4 and 4 has not yet linked the rods to the number.

1:mental-math-to-100#subtract-tens-from-.title: Subtract tens from tens
1:mental-math-to-100#subtract-tens-from-.objective: Children subtract multiples of 10 from multiples of 10 in the range 10 to 90 (70 − 30) by crossing out ten-rods, and explain why 7 tens take away 3 tens leaves 4 tens.

note.mistake: Children cross out the right number of rods and then write how many rods are left (4) in place of the number (40). Others count back by ones from 70 and lose count. Some count the crossed-out rods again when they count what is left.
note.words: Say the problem in tens: "70 is 7 tens. Take away 3 tens. Cross out three rods. How many tens are left? Four tens is forty." Then link it to a fact they know: "7 − 3 = 4, so 7 tens − 3 tens = 4 tens." Show it in the Number Hotel too: from 70 the elevator goes down three floors, 60, 50, 40.
note.watch: Watch who uses 7 − 3 and who counts each rod that is left by tens. Check the answers for a missing zero. Ask a child who is done early to solve 60 − 20 with no picture and to tell you how.

2:column-method#subtract-three-digit-num.title: Subtract three-digit numbers with regrouping
2:column-method#subtract-three-digit-num.objective: Children subtract within 1,000 in columns when a ten or a hundred must be regrouped (432 − 151), and check each answer by adding.

note.mistake: The common error is to subtract the smaller digit from the larger one in every column (432 − 151 = 321). Children who do regroup often forget to write one fewer ten or one fewer hundred, or regroup a ten when there are already enough ones.
note.words: Start at the ones each time and ask: "Enough ones? If not, regroup: trade one ten for ten ones. One ten fewer, ten more ones." Then the tens: "Enough tens? If not, trade one hundred for ten tens." Have children cross out the digit and write the new one above it.
note.watch: Watch the first step of each problem: does the child ask "enough ones?" or just subtract? Have every child check two answers by adding the answer and the number taken away. Level 1 takes away a two-digit number: use it for children who are not yet sure of the columns. On level 3 children regroup twice in the same problem, a ten and a hundred.

K:count-how-many#count-and-write-up-to-2.title: Count and write how many: up to 20
K:count-how-many#count-and-write-up-to-2.objective: Children count 11 to 20 objects arranged in rows of five, touching each one once, and write the number.

note.mistake: Children skip a picture or count one twice when their finger and their voice get out of step, most often at the start of a new row. Some lose the counting order in the teens (they skip 13 or 15, or say "ten-teen"), so the last number is wrong even when every picture was touched once. When they write, some reverse the digits (41 for 14).
note.words: Say: "Touch each one as you count. Go along the row, then start the next row at the left." Ask: "Two full rows are how many? Ten. So you can start at ten: 11, 12, 13." Let children put a cube on each picture and move the cubes into two ten-frames. On the ten-frame tool, switch to two frames: fill one frame for the first two rows (ten) and put the rest on the second frame: "Ten and 3 more is 13."
note.watch: Watch the child's finger at each new row. Ask "How many?" again when the child has finished: a child who counts all over again does not yet know that the last number said tells how many. Check the written number against the number the child says.

K:compare-groups#match-them-up.title: Match them up: more, fewer, or the same
K:compare-groups#match-them-up.objective: Children match the pictures in two rows one-to-one and say which row has more, which has fewer, or that both rows have the same number.

note.mistake: Children pick a row by looking, without pairing: they choose the row with the bigger pictures, or, with loose cubes, the row that is spread out longer. Some draw two lines to one picture or skip a picture, so the wrong number of pictures is left over, or the wrong row seems to have more. Many can say "more" and do not yet use "fewer".
note.words: Use cubes of two colors first: "Give every red cube a blue partner. Are any left over? That color has more. The other color has fewer." On the page say: "Draw one line from each picture to a partner. No picture gets two lines. Some pictures may have no partner. The row with pictures left over has more. No picture left over? Both rows have the same number: color the star."
note.watch: Watch that no picture has two lines and that only the extra pictures at the end of the longer row have no line. Ask about every task: "Which row has more? Which has fewer?" On the ten-frame, show two groups of up to five: one color in the top row and the other color in the bottom row, so the counters left over stand out. For rows of 6 to 10, use two trains of cubes side by side.

1:fact-families#think-addition-to-subtra.title: Think addition to subtract
1:fact-families#think-addition-to-subtra.objective: Children subtract from numbers 11 to 18 by finding the unknown addend, for example solving 13 − 8 by asking 8 + ? = 13.

note.mistake: Children count back by ones from 13 and lose track, or they do not see that 13 − 8 and 8 + ? = 13 ask for the same number. Some write one number in the subtraction and another in the addition; a frequent one is adding the two numbers they see in 8 + □ = 13 and writing 21 in the box.
note.words: Point to the number bond: "13 is the whole. 8 is one part. What is the other part?" Say: "I don't have to count back. I can ask: 8 and how many more make 13?" Count up through ten: "8 and 2 make 10, and 3 more make 13. 2 and 3 make 5." Then read all three: "8 + 5 = 13, so 13 − 8 = 5."
note.watch: Watch who counts back and who counts up from the part. Check that the same number is written in all three places on a card. The easier page has wholes to 10: use it for children who still need to learn what the number bond shows. The harder page has no number bond. On the number balance, put 13 on one side and 8 on the other and ask: "What must we add to the 8 side to make it level?" Add 5: 8 + 5 = 13, so 13 − 8 = 5.

3:fraction-number-line#unit-fractions-on.title: Unit fractions on the number line
3:fraction-number-line#unit-fractions-on.objective: Children see the distance from 0 to 1 on a number line partitioned into 2, 3, 4, 6, or 8 equal parts and name the endpoint of the first part as 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/6, or 1/8. Then they count equal parts from 0 to place a fraction such as 3/8 on the line.

note.mistake: Children count the tick marks instead of the equal parts, so on a line partitioned into fourths they write 1/5 (five marks) or 1/3 (three marks between 0 and 1). Some write the fraction upside down (4/1). Many think 1/8 is greater than 1/4 because 8 is greater than 4.
note.words: Say: "Count the jumps from 0 to 1, not the marks. How many equal parts? Four. Each part is one fourth." Point to the dot: "The dot is at the end of the first part. That is 1 of 4 equal parts: 1 on top, 4 on the bottom." Compare two lines: "Which first part is longer, one fourth or one eighth? Why?" For the second worksheet say: "Three eighths. Each jump is one eighth. Start at 0 and count three jumps: one eighth, two eighths, three eighths. Draw the dot there."
note.watch: Watch what the child counts: parts or marks. Check the bottom number first: it must be the number of equal parts between 0 and 1. On the second worksheet the fraction is printed and the child draws the dot. Most of its fractions are not unit fractions (3/8, 2/3, 4/6): watch that the child counts that many parts from 0 and does not stop at the first mark. The harder page of the first worksheet has fractions such as 3/4.

1:mental-math-to-100#add-tens-and-ones.title: Add tens and ones, then put them together
1:mental-math-to-100#add-tens-and-ones.objective: Children add two two-digit numbers within 100 when the ones make a new ten (47 + 38) by adding the tens, adding the ones, and adding the two partial sums (70 + 15).

note.mistake: When the ones add up to more than nine, children write the two sums side by side, so 47 + 38 becomes 715, or they drop the new ten and answer 75. Some add the tens as if they were ones and write 4 + 3 = 7 instead of 40 + 30 = 70.
note.words: Build 47 in the Place Value Lab and add 38: first 3 tens, then 8 ones. Say: "4 tens and 3 tens are 7 tens: 70. 7 ones and 8 ones are 15 ones. 70 and 15 make 85." Ask: "What is 15? One ten and five ones. Where does that ten go?" Let children draw sticks and dots for one problem on scrap paper and circle ten dots to make a new stick.
note.watch: Check the first box of each problem: for 40 + 30, did the child write 70 and not 7? The easier page has problems with no new ten, such as 34 + 25. On the harder page children write the tens and ones themselves; the first problem shows how. Check there that the first line says 40 + 30 and not 4 + 3. Not every problem on the harder page makes a new ten; ask children to say which ones will before they add. Have children test an answer against an estimate: 47 + 38 is close to 50 + 40.

3:times-tables#break-a-hard-fact.title: Break a hard fact into two easy ones
3:times-tables#break-a-hard-fact.objective: Children split an array for a fact with 7, 8, or 9 into two arrays they know and add the two products, such as 7 × 8 = 5 × 8 + 2 × 8 = 40 + 16.

note.mistake: Children cut the array into two parts they do not know either, such as 7 × 8 into 4 × 8 and 3 × 8, and then skip-count both parts. Others write both products correctly and forget to add them. Some cut between columns, so the two parts no longer fit the number sentence under the array.
note.words: On the Baking Tray, set 7 rows of 8 buns and break the tray after the fifth row. Say: "5 rows of 8 is 40. 2 rows of 8 is 16. 7 × 8 is 40 + 16, so 56." Ask: "Where will you draw your line so that you know both parts?" Push the pieces back together and ask: "Did the number of buns change?"
note.watch: Look at where each child draws the line: a cut after 5 rows gives a 5s fact and a small part of 2, 3, or 4 rows. A child who does not know the small part yet can build it from the 2s: 2 × 8 is 16, so 4 × 8 is double, 32, and 3 × 8 is 16 and 8 more, 24. The easier page has the line and the two smaller facts printed. On the harder page children cut the same array in two different ways and see that the total stays the same.

1:fluency-within-20#make-ten-sums-11-to-.title: Make ten to add: sums from 11 to 18
1:fluency-within-20#make-ten-sums-11-to-.objective: Children add two one-digit numbers with a sum from 11 to 18 by splitting one of them to make ten, such as 8 + 6 = 8 + 2 + 4 = 14, and begin to see the two jumps in their heads.

note.mistake: Second graders who learned this last year often still count on by ones under their breath and fill in the two parts afterward, so the page looks right and the fact is not getting any faster. Others stall when the first number is the small one, as in 6 + 9, because they have only ever made ten from 8 or 9.
note.words: Write 8 + 6 on the board. On the open number line, mark 8 and ask: "How far is it to ten? What is left of the 6?" Draw the two jumps and say: "8 and 2 make 10, and 4 more make 14." Then cover the line: "Can you see the jumps in your head? Try 7 + 5." Have children say the two parts aloud before they say the sum.
note.watch: Watch for lips moving: a child who counts on by ones lands on the right sum and never stops at ten. Ask that child for the partner that makes 10 before each problem. The page always starts from the first number; after 6 + 9 ask: "Which number would you rather start from?" Starting from the 9 takes only 1 to reach ten. The page has one worked problem and only three to solve, so keep going aloud: give 9 + 4, 7 + 6, and 5 + 8 without a number line and have children say the two parts before the sum. Note the facts a child answers at once: those need no jumps anymore.

1:near-doubles#doubles-and-near-doubles.title: Doubles and near doubles
1:near-doubles#doubles-and-near-doubles.objective: Children say the doubles up to 9 + 9 from memory and use them to solve near doubles, such as 7 + 8 = 7 + 7 + 1 = 15.

note.mistake: Children know the small doubles and stall at 7 + 7, 8 + 8, and 9 + 9, so the near doubles built on them (7 + 8, 8 + 9) turn back into counting. When the larger number comes first, as in 9 + 8, some double the 9 and still add one, and get 19.
note.words: Start with the doubles alone. Put 7 counters on the near leaf of the Doubling Mirror and ask: "What will the double be?" Close the tray and count on from 7 as the counters land on the far leaf: 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14. Do 6, 8, and 9 the same way until the answers come at once. Then: "7 + 8. Which double is inside? 7 + 7 is 14, and one more is 15." For 9 + 8 ask: "Which number do we double so that one more is left over?"
note.watch: On the page for everyone the child writes the double: check that it is the double of the smaller number, because every problem adds one. The easier page prints the double. The harder page has problems that take one away from the double of the larger number (6 + 7 = 7 + 7 − 1); use it with children who finish the page for everyone quickly. A child who cannot say 8 + 8 at once needs the doubles, not more near doubles.

1:fluency-within-20#use-ten-to-subtract.title: Use ten to subtract
1:fluency-within-20#use-ten-to-subtract.objective: Children subtract a one-digit number from a number from 11 to 18 by going back to ten first, such as 15 − 7 = 15 − 5 − 2 = 8.

note.mistake: Children count back by ones and end one off, because they say the starting number as the first count (15, 14, 13 …). Others subtract the smaller ones digit from the larger one, no matter which number it belongs to, and solve 15 − 7 as 7 − 5 = 2, so 12.
note.words: On the rekenrek, show 15 as a full row of ten and 5 beads on the second row. Say: "Take away 7. First the 5 on the second row: now we are at ten. 7 is 5 and 2, so 2 more come off the top row. 8 are left." Ask before every problem: "How many do you take away to get back to ten? How many are still to go?" Then show the same thing on the number line of the page: one jump from 15 back to 10, and one jump of 2 more back to 8.
note.watch: Watch the first box: it is always the ones digit of the starting number (for 14 − 6 it is 4). A child who writes another number there has not stopped at ten. The easier page shows the first problem worked with its two jumps. The harder page asks for the same two jumps with larger numbers and no worked problem (62 − 6: back to 60, then 4 more). These numbers go past 20; the two jumps are the same. Give it to children who no longer need to draw the jumps within 20.

1:fact-families#think-addition-and-daily.title: Think addition to subtract, and start the daily facts
1:fact-families#think-addition-and-daily.objective: Children solve subtraction facts within 20 by thinking of the addition fact (15 − 9 as 9 + ? = 15), and begin a five-minute daily facts routine that runs all year.

note.mistake: Children treat 15 − 9 and 9 + ? = 15 as two separate problems: they count back for the first and count up for the second, and sometimes write two different numbers. In the daily facts, children who feel pushed to be fast stop thinking and guess.
note.words: On the Number Balance, put 15 on one side and 9 on the other. Ask: "What do we add to the 9 to make the beam level?" Say: "9 and 1 make 10, and 5 more make 15. So 9 + 6 = 15, and 15 − 9 = 6." For the daily facts say: "Five minutes, every day. I show a fact, you write the answer and hold it up. For one or two of them, someone tells how they got it: make ten, a double, back to ten, or think addition."
note.watch: The page for everyone has no number bond: check that the child writes the same number in both number sentences of a problem. The easier page draws the bond for children who need to see the whole and its two parts. For the daily facts, show eight to ten facts within 20 each day, one at a time, mixing addition and subtraction; in the first weeks take them from this unit. Give children about three seconds, have them answer on whiteboards, and do not time or score them. Keep a list of the facts many children still have to figure out and bring those back the next day; take a fact off the list when almost everyone answers it right away. The lesson has no worksheet for the daily facts.

1:word-problems#find-the-missing-part.title: Find the missing part
1:word-problems#find-the-missing-part.objective: Children solve put-together stories within 20 in which the total and one part are known: they mark the missing part with a question mark in a bar model and write an equation for the story.

note.mistake: Children add the two numbers they see (12 in all and 7 in the red box become 19), because nothing is taken away in the story. Others write the total in one of the small parts of the bar.
note.words: Open the Number Bonds Board, set the number to 10, tap counters across until the left part holds 6, and put the cloth over the right part: "Two boxes have 10 apples in all. 6 are in the red box. What do we know? What are we looking for?" Draw the bar on the board: "The long bar is all 10. The two short bars are the parts. One part is 6. The other part is our question mark." Write 6 + ? = 10, then take the cloth off.
note.watch: On the page for everyone the total is between 11 and 20. The easier page stays within 10 and its first story is worked, so a child sees what goes where; the harder page uses whole tens (70 in all, 30 in the red box). Check the bar first: the total belongs in the long bar. For 12 in all and 7 in one part, the key writes 7 + 5 = 12; 12 − 7 = 5 is just as correct. A child who answers 19 has added: build the 12 with counters and cover the 7.

1:word-problems#what-happened-in-the-mid.title: What happened in the middle?
1:word-problems#what-happened-in-the-mid.objective: Children solve stories within 20 in which the start and the end are known and the change is missing (some came or some left): they mark the change with a question mark in a bar model and write an equation for the story.

note.mistake: Children add the two numbers in the story no matter what happened. In a story where some leave, many write the starting number in a small part of the bar, but in those stories the start is the whole.
note.words: Open The Gap and choose "up to sixteen" in its settings. Count the marks on the ground together (say there are 8), tap "Show the gap," and count again (say 13). Write both numbers: "Did some come or did some leave? How many?" Take a child's number and try it. Then draw the bar: "More came, so 13 is all of them. 8 were there at the start. The question mark is what came." Write 8 + ? = 13. When some left, the first count is all of them.
note.watch: The page for everyone has one story in which some more come and two in which some leave, with a larger number from 11 to 20. The easier page stays within 10 and its first story is worked; the harder page uses whole tens. Ask "Which number is all of them?" before the child writes: in 8 + ? = 13 it is the end, in 12 − ? = 7 it is the start. Either true equation counts (13 − 8 = 5 for 8 + ? = 13).

1:word-problems#how-many-more-how-many-f.title: How many more? How many fewer?
1:word-problems#how-many-more-how-many-f.objective: Children compare two amounts within 20 in a story, shown as two lined-up rows of pictures, and find how many more or how many fewer.

note.mistake: Children hear "more" and add the two amounts (12 and 7 become 19), or they answer with the larger amount. "How many fewer" is harder than "how many more", although it is the same difference.
note.words: Open The Planks and drag the two planks to 12 and 7 before you say anything: "Mia has 12 stickers. Ben has 7. Where do you see how many more?" Let the class say how long the piece under the bracket is, then move it to the end of the short plank: "Mia has 5 more than Ben. Ben has 5 fewer than Mia. Ben needs 5 more to have as many as Mia." Say all three sentences for every pair.
note.watch: The page shows the two amounts as two rows of pictures that start at the same line. Have the child circle the pictures that stick out before writing the number in the box; the dotted space is for a drawing or an equation. On the page for everyone the larger amount is 11 to 14 in both stories; the easier page stays within 10; the harder page has three stories. A child who writes 19 has added: cover what both rows have and ask what is left. Children can also practice story problems on screen.

2:two-step-word-problems#one-step-storie.title: One-step stories with a bar model
2:two-step-word-problems#one-step-storie.objective: Children solve one-step story problems within 100 in which the end, the change, or a part is missing, with a bar model and an equation, and write the question for a story that has none.

note.mistake: With two-digit numbers children stop reading and just compute: they add the two numbers in every story. When more are added and the story asks for the change (34 + ? = 52), they write 34 + 52.
note.words: Open The Missing Question and tell a story with no numbers, for example: "There are some pencils in a box. Sam puts in some more." Ask: "What could we ask?" Collect their questions, then tell the numbers one at a time. Draw the bar: "Which number is all of them? Which part do we know? Where is the question mark?" Write 34 + ? = 52 first, then the equation you solve, 52 − 34 = 18.
note.watch: On the bar-model page one story asks for the end and two ask for the change; its easier page asks for the end in all three stories and the first is worked; its harder page asks for the change or for a missing part. The second page, Question, Equation, Answer, has three more stories and no bar. On the page for everyone one question is missing and the child writes it: accept any question that needs both numbers ("How many are still on the table?"). One story there compares two boxes. Either true equation counts.

1:add-three-addends#stories-with-three-n.title: Stories with three numbers
1:add-three-addends#stories-with-three-n.objective: Children solve story problems that add three numbers with a total up to 20, with a drawing and an equation, and look for two numbers that make ten before they add.

note.mistake: Children add the first two numbers and stop, or they count all three groups by ones and lose count. Few look at all three numbers before they start, so a pair that makes ten goes unused.
note.words: Write a story on the board: "There are 4 pencils on the table, 7 in a box, and 6 in a basket. How many pencils are there in all?" Draw three groups of dots and write 4 + 7 + 6. Ask: "Which two numbers make ten?" Circle 4 and 6 and write 10 + 7 = 17. Then point to the groups in another order: "Did the total change?" Any order gives the same total, so we can start with the ten.
note.watch: On the page for everyone every story has two numbers that make ten, in a different place each time: the child draws the three groups in the box, writes the three numbers in the frame, and adds. The easier page has totals from 6 to 10 and no ten to find. On the harder page one story has a ten, one has a double (such as 3 + 8 + 3), and one has neither, so the child has to look first. The second page, Add Three Numbers, has twelve problems with no story. On its page for everyone each has a pair that makes ten; on its harder page only half do. A child who adds from left to right and is correct has done nothing wrong: ask, "Is there a faster way?"

2:two-step-word-problems#what-was-there-.title: What was there at the start?
2:two-step-word-problems#what-was-there-.objective: Children solve one-step story problems within 100 in which the starting amount is unknown, with a bar model and an equation.

note.mistake: Children do what the story says: when 17 more are put in, they add 17 to the number they see, and when some are taken out, they subtract. In these stories the words point the wrong way: "takes out 25, now there are 38 left" calls for adding.
note.words: Open The Missing Question and choose "one thing happened". Tell a story with no numbers: "There are some pencils in a box. Sam puts in some more. Now there are a lot." Ask, "What could we ask?" until someone asks what was there at the start (ask it yourself if no one does); choose that place as the one to work out and give the other two numbers (the tool goes up to twenty). Then draw the bar model with two-digit numbers: "45 are in the box now. 17 were put in. The question mark is what was there before." Write ? + 17 = 45, then 45 − 17 = 28.
note.watch: On the page for everyone all three stories ask for the start. When some were added, the end is the whole (? + 17 = 45). When some were taken away, the start is the whole, so the question mark goes in the long bar and the child adds (? − 25 = 38, so 38 + 25 = 63). On the easier page every number is a multiple of 10 and the first story is worked. On the harder page one story asks for the change, so the child has to read which number is missing. Accept either equation: ? + 17 = 45 or 45 − 17 = 28.

2:two-step-word-problems#compare-stories.title: Compare stories: more and fewer
2:two-step-word-problems#compare-stories.objective: Children solve compare stories within 100 in which the difference, the larger amount, or the smaller amount is unknown, with two bars and an equation.

note.mistake: Children add when they read "more" and subtract when they read "fewer" without asking which box has more. That fails when the story says "That is 29 more than in the blue box": the red box has more, so the blue box has fewer, and the child has to subtract.
note.words: Open The Planks and drag the two planks to 15 and 9: "The red box has 15. The blue box has 9. Which box has more? How many more?" Carry away the piece that sticks out and say all three sentences: "The red box has 6 more. The blue box has 6 fewer. 9 and 6 more make 15." Then draw two bars on the board: "There are 85 oranges in a red box. That is 29 more than in the blue box. Which bar is longer?" The dashed piece is the piece that sticks out, drawn next to the short bar. Write 85 in the long bar, 29 in the dashed piece, a question mark in the short bar, and 85 − 29 = 56: "The blue box has 56."
note.watch: On the page for everyone, the bars are drawn: the longer bar is the box with more, and the dashed piece next to the shorter bar is the difference. In all three stories, "more" means add and "fewer" means subtract, so a correct page does not yet show that the child compared. On the easier page, every number is a multiple of 10 and the first story is done. On the harder page, two stories say "That is … more than" or "That is … fewer than," and the child draws the bars next to the red and blue squares. Ask "Which box has more?" before any number is written.

2:two-step-word-problems#two-step-storie.title: Two-step stories
2:two-step-word-problems#two-step-storie.objective: Children solve story problems within 100 that need two steps of adding or subtracting, and write an equation for each step.

note.mistake: Children do one step and stop, or they add all three numbers no matter what happens in the story. Many start the second step from the first number of the story again instead of from the answer to the first step.
note.words: Tell a story in two parts and stop in the middle: "There are 36 apples in a box. Mia takes out 21." Ask, "How many are in the box now?" Write 36 − 21 = 15 and circle the 15. "Then Mia puts in 27. Which number do we start from now?" Write 15 + 27 = 42 under it and draw an arrow from the 15 to the start of the second line. Have a child retell the whole story with the numbers.
note.watch: On the page for everyone, the two steps are printed as a) and b) with boxes: the answer to step a) is written again at the start of step b). The easier page has two stories with multiples of 10. On the harder page, only the answer box is printed, and the child works out the two steps in the dotted space. Where two children take some, adding the two amounts first and subtracting once is right, too. The second page, Two-Step Word Problems, has three stories within 20 with the steps printed: start there with children who are not sure. A child who adds all three numbers needs to act the story out with counters and small numbers.

3:two-step-word-problems#two-step-storie.title: Two-step stories: add and subtract
3:two-step-word-problems#two-step-storie.objective: Children solve two-step story problems with adding and subtracting within 1,000 and show each step as an equation.

note.mistake: Children add every number they see, or they finish the first step and write that number as the answer. With three-digit numbers, some lose track of the story while they regroup, or carry the wrong number from step a) into step b).
note.words: Tell a story in two parts and stop in the middle: "A store has 356 pencils. A truck brings 124 more. How many pencils does the store have now?" Write 356 + 124 = 480 and circle the 480. "Then the store sells 213. Which number do we start from now?" Write 480 − 213 = 267 under it and draw an arrow from the 480 to the second line. Ask, "Does 267 make sense? The store sold more than the truck brought, so it has fewer than at the start." If the regrouping gets in the way, do one subtraction on the Exchange Machine first (it deals its own numbers).
note.watch: On the page for everyone, the two steps are printed as a) and b) with boxes, and the dotted space is for the written work.
