It has three stories from four kinds: a store that gets a delivery and then sells, a market that sells and then gets a delivery, workers who pack on three days, and a truck that leaves things at two stores. The easier page has two stories with numbers that end in 0 (380 + 270). On the harder page, only the answer box is printed, and the child finds the two steps; there, in a truck story, adding the two amounts first and subtracting once is right, too.

3:two-step-word-problems#two-step-storie.title: Two-step stories: multiply or divide
3:two-step-word-problems#two-step-storie.objective: Children solve two-step story problems in which one step multiplies or divides within 100 and the other adds or subtracts.

note.mistake: Children miss the word "each" and add: for "There are 6 baskets. Each basket holds 8 medals. 3 are taken out," they compute 6 + 8 − 3. Others multiply and stop. In the sharing stories, some divide the first number they see before they have asked what is being shared.
note.words: On the Baking Tray, set 4 rows of 6 buns: "The baker made 4 rows with 6 buns in each row. How many buns? Which fact?" Write 4 × 6 = 24. "She sells 5." The tray cannot take buns away, so write it: "What happens to the 24?" 24 − 5 = 19. Then tell a sharing story without the tray: "There are 12 pens in a red box and 8 in a blue box. 4 children share all of them fairly. What is being shared? All the pens. What first?" Write 12 + 8 = 20, then 20 ÷ 4 = 5.
note.watch: On the page for everyone, the steps are printed as a) and b): one story multiplies first, one divides first, and one adds the things in two boxes first and then shares. The easier page has two stories that multiply first, with factors from 2 to 5. On the harder page, only the answer box is printed; one story may be "keeps some and shares the rest," where subtracting comes first. A child who cannot say what each number counts (baskets, things in one basket, things taken out) draws the story in the dotted space first.

3:two-step-word-problems#an-equation-wit.title: A letter for the unknown and an estimate to check the answer
3:two-step-word-problems#an-equation-wit.objective: Children write one equation with a letter for the unknown for a two-step story problem, solve it, and check the answer against an estimate from rounded numbers.

note.mistake: Children treat the estimate as one more exercise and never compare it with the answer. Many round the exact answer after they have computed it, which checks nothing. Some think n is the same number in every story; it is only a name for the number we do not know yet.
note.words: Write the store story as one line: 356 + 124 − 213 = n. "n is the number of pencils the store has at the end." Estimate before computing. On the Rounding Hill, choose the ground between two hundreds, shift the hill to 300 and 400, move the boulder to 360 (the spot nearest 356), and let go: it settles into 400. "356 rounds to 400, 124 to 100, 213 to 200. 400 + 100 − 200 = 300." Compute n = 267: "Is 267 near 300? Yes." Then write n = 693: "A child got this. Near 300? No. What went wrong?" (The 213 was added.)
note.watch: On the easier page, the equation is printed and the estimate has a frame of boxes for the rounded numbers. On the page for everyone, the child writes both on lines. The harder page has three stories; the last one prints a child's finished answer, which is right on some pages and far off on others: the child estimates, marks yes or no, and then finds n. No number on these pages ends in 45 to 55, so no one has to argue about a halfway number. A right answer is never more than 100 from the estimate, and a wrong printed answer is at least 200 away: "near" means within about 100.

3:area-model#area-of-a-rectangle-multipl.title: Area of a rectangle: multiply the side lengths
3:area-model#area-of-a-rectangle-multipl.objective: Children find the area of a rectangle by multiplying its two side lengths and say the area with its square unit (24 square feet).

note.mistake: Children add the two side lengths, or add all four sides (they find the perimeter). Others multiply correctly and say the unit of length: "24 feet" for 24 square feet.
note.words: On the Baking Tray, set 4 rows of 6 buns: "How many buns? We don't have to count them one by one: 4 rows of 6 is 4 × 6." Give the tray a quarter turn: "6 rows of 4. Still 24." Draw a rectangle on the board and write 6 ft on top and 4 ft on the left side: "This time no squares are drawn. Picture squares 1 foot on each side. How many fit along the top? How many rows?" Write 4 × 6 = 24 and say the unit: "24 square feet. A square foot is a square that is 1 foot long and 1 foot wide."
note.watch: On the easier page, the squares are still drawn in each rectangle, so a child can check the product by counting. On the page for everyone, only the two side lengths are written. Either order of the two factors is right (6 × 4 or 4 × 6). On the harder page, the sides go from 4 to 10, and two cards show a question mark on one side and print the area ("Area = 54 square meters"): the child finds the side. A child who multiplies 9 × 54 has not read the equation: ask, "What number times 9 makes 54?" The unit changes from card to card, and the area unit is printed with the boxes: have children read it aloud with their answer.

3:area-model#area-of-an-l-shape.title: Area of an L-shape
3:area-model#area-of-an-l-shape.objective: Children cut an L-shaped figure into two rectangles, find the area of each by multiplying, and add the two areas.

note.mistake: Children multiply the two longest sides, as if the figure were a full rectangle. On the page without a grid, they use a side length of the whole figure for one of the parts (for example, 10 where the part is only 6 wide).
note.words: On the Baking Tray, set 5 rows of 6 buns and crack the tray after the third row: "Two trays: 3 rows of 6 and 2 rows of 6. 18 + 12 = 30. Nothing was lost." The tray cannot make an L-shape, so go to the board and draw one on a grid: "This is not one rectangle. It is two rectangles pushed together. Where can one straight cut make two rectangles?" Draw the cut, name the parts A and B, write a product for each, and add. Cut the same figure the other way and add again: "The same area. Either cut is right."
note.watch: On the easier page, the cut is drawn and the parts are named A and B. On the page for everyone, the figure is on a grid without the cut: the child draws the cut, and either of the two cuts is right. On the harder page, there is no grid and the six side lengths are written at the sides. Every length the child needs is printed, for either cut; nothing has to be subtracted. Have the child trace each part with a finger and say its two sides before writing a product. A child who takes the missing corner away from the full rectangle is right; ask for a cut as well, because the boxes add.

3:perimeter#find-the-missing-side.title: Perimeter: find the missing side
3:perimeter#find-the-missing-side.objective: Children find one unknown side length of a figure from its perimeter and the other side lengths, and write an equation with a letter for the unknown side.

note.mistake: Children add the side lengths they see and write that sum as the answer, or they add the perimeter to it. In the rectangle with one side length given, they subtract that side once instead of twice, or they subtract it twice and write what is left as n without halving it.
note.words: On All the Way Round, let the strand lie down: "The distance all the way around is one length." The tool shows no sides and no numbers, so go to the board. Draw a triangle with sides 10 ft and 6 ft and one side n: "The perimeter is 24 feet. Picture its strand laid straight: 24 feet long." Draw the strand as a bar cut into three pieces: 10, 6, n. Write 10 + 6 + n = 24. "10 + 6 is 16. What do we add to 16 to make 24?" n = 8. Check by adding all three sides.
note.watch: On the easier page, the equation is printed under each figure and the child finds n. On the page for everyone, the child writes the equation on the line. The page has triangles, four-sided figures, and five-sided figures. On the harder page, the perimeters go up to 100, one figure is an L-shape with six sides, and two rectangles show one side length and the letter n on two sides. The printed side counts twice; what is left is n + n, so the child still has to split it in two (one side 9, perimeter 30: 9 + 9 + n + n = 30; 12 is left; n = 6). The figures are drawn in proportion (not actual size), so a child can see whether an answer looks right.

2:add-with-blocks#add-two-two-digit-numb.title: Add two two-digit numbers and make a new ten
2:add-with-blocks#add-two-two-digit-numb.objective: Children add two two-digit numbers when the ones make a new ten (36 + 28), with a drawing of sticks and dots on a tens-and-ones mat, and tell why the new ten joins the tens.

note.mistake: Children add each column and write both totals side by side, so 36 + 28 becomes 514 (5 tens, 14 ones). Others circle ten dots and forget to draw the new stick, or draw it and still count the circled dots as ones.
note.words: On the Place Value Lab, build 36 with "Add a ten" and "Add a one." Then add 28 more: two tens and eight ones. "How many ones now? 14. Can we write 14 in the ones place?" The lab asks, "Ten ones! Can you make a ten?" Tap "Make a ten!" and say: "Ten ones make one ten. It joins the tens: 6 tens and 4 ones, 64." Do the same problem on the board with sticks and dots, the dots in rows of five: circle ten dots, draw one new stick, and ask a child to tell why you drew it.
note.watch: On the easier page, both numbers are drawn on the mat, the second under the first (in green); the child circles ten dots, draws the new stick, and counts. On the page for everyone, the mat is empty: the child draws both numbers first, and every problem makes a new ten. On the harder page, two of the six problems make no new ten, so the child has to look before circling. In the boxes under the mat, ten circled dots count as one ten: 6 tens and 4 ones, not 5 tens and 14 ones. When the ones make exactly ten (41 + 29), the child writes 7 tens and 0 ones; watch for an empty ones box.

2:subtract-with-blocks#subtract-and-open.title: Subtract and open a ten
2:subtract-with-blocks#subtract-and-open.objective: Children subtract within 100 when there are not enough ones (52 − 27) by regrouping: they open one ten into ten ones in a drawing of sticks and dots.

note.mistake: Children subtract the smaller ones digit from the larger, no matter which number it is in, so 52 − 27 becomes 35. Others draw the ten dots but do not cross out the stick they opened, so they take 2 tens from 5, not from 4. Some open a ten in every problem, even when there are enough ones.
note.words: The Exchange Machine opens with 48 − 23. "Start at the ones. Are there enough to take 3 away? Yes." Tap "Another sum": 42 − 17. "Enough ones to take 7 away? No, there are only 2." Tap the tens column: one ten crosses over and comes apart into ten ones, and the 4 is crossed out. "We regrouped: 3 tens and 12 ones. It is still 42." Draw the same on the board: four sticks and two dots. Cross out one stick, draw ten dots for it, then cross out 7 dots and 1 stick. "What is left? 2 tens and 5 ones: 25."
note.watch: The easier page takes away a one-digit number; the page for everyone, a two-digit number. On the harder page, the mat is empty and the child draws the first number. Every page has problems that need no ten opened (two on the first two pages, one on the harder page): there the child marks "yes" and only crosses out. Check the yes/no mark first; a wrong mark explains a wrong answer. A first number with no ones (50 − 4) always needs a ten opened; watch for 54. Have children say what the mat shows after the trade ("4 tens and 10 ones") before they cross anything out.

2:column-method#add-three-and-four-two-d.title: Add three and four two-digit numbers
2:column-method#add-three-and-four-two-d.objective: Children add three or four two-digit numbers with a sum within 100 in columns, look for ones that make ten, and write the new tens above the tens column.

note.mistake: Children add the ones, get 18 or 23, and write both digits under the line, so the answer has three digits. Others write the new ten above the tens and forget to add it. When the ones add up to 20 or more, they still write 1 in the small box.
note.words: On the Exchange Machine, tap "Another sum" five times, until 38 + 25 appears. Fill the outlines in the ones column: "8 and 5 make 13. Only one digit fits under the line." Tap the ones column: ten gather into one new ten on the left. The machine adds two numbers only, so go to the board. Write 18 + 36 + 24 in columns. "Look at the ones: 8, 6, 4. Do two of them make ten? 6 and 4. Ten and 8 more is 18." Write 8 under the ones and a small 1 above the tens. "Now the tens: 1 new ten, and 1, 3, 2. That makes 7 tens." 78.
note.watch: On the easier page, there are six problems with three numbers; the ones make no new ten and there is no small box. On the page for everyone, four problems have three numbers and four have four; in each, two of the ones digits make ten, and one new ten goes in the small box. On the harder page, every problem has four numbers and the ones make one or two new tens (8 + 9 + 6 + 0 = 23: write 3 under the ones and 2 in the small box). When the ones make exactly 20, a 0 goes under the ones. Ask children to say the sum of the ones before they write. Have them check by adding from the bottom up.
